pitfalls-of-vibe-testing.explain:
## What it is

**Vibe testing** means trying a handful of prompts, reading the outputs, and deciding it "feels good". It is how most LLM projects start, and it fails predictably.

- **Tiny, biased sample**: you test the prompts you thought of, which are the ones you already optimised for.
- **No memory**: you cannot tell whether last week's prompt change helped or silently broke a case you checked then.
- **Noise looks like signal**: outputs are sampled, so one good run proves little. Ten runs of five prompts is still only fifty readings with no baseline.
- **Reviewer drift**: your standard changes with mood and fatigue.

Example: you tweak a system prompt, three demo questions look better, you ship. A week later support finds the model now refuses a whole class of refund questions. Nothing recorded that case.

The fix is not abandoning judgement but making it repeatable: a versioned dataset, explicit criteria, scored runs you can diff. In interviews, say vibe testing is fine for exploration and fatal as a release gate.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Vibe testing is trying a handful of prompts and shipping because it “feels good.” It is how most LLM features start and how silent regressions ship. Air Canada’s chatbot inventing a bereavement policy is the usual case study: a fluent answer, no stored cases, a real refund.

Interviews: vibe is exploration; it is fatal as a release gate.

## How it works + one small example

Keep vibe for the first afternoon. The same day, freeze 20–30 cases with expected shape or a rubric. Next change runs the set. The Air Canada-style failure is a case you add after you read the news: “policy questions must cite the page or refuse.”

Reviewer drift is real: score with a checklist, not a mood.

## Failure modes

1. **Shipping on five demo wins.**

2. **No stored baseline so you cannot diff last week.**

3. **Treating a news incident as “won’t happen here” instead of a case.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Vibe testing is for exploration. A release gate is a versioned set with a baseline. Fluent is not correct — ask Air Canada.

## A concrete walk-through

You tweak a system prompt; three demos look better. The frozen set drops 8 points on refunds. You do not ship. A week later that drop would have been the support queue.

## Interview follow-up

They ask for the case study. Name a public chatbot policy failure and the missing artefact: a stored case with a citation rule.

## What I would measure

Share of changes gated by the set, regressions caught pre-ship, demo-only ships (0).

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Share of changes gated by the set, regressions caught pre-ship, demo-only ships (0). That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Vibe: small biased sample, no baseline, reviewer drift. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.
keyPoints: Vibe: small biased sample, no baseline, reviewer drift.
OK for exploration; fatal as a gate.
Store cases the day a second person uses the app.
Score with a checklist, not a mood.
Vibe testing has small biased samples and no baseline
Single good outputs prove little when generation is sampled

questions.q: Why is vibe testing a poor release gate for an LLM feature?
questions.a: It samples a few prompts the author chose, so coverage and selection are biased. Outputs are stochastic so single runs are noisy. There is no stored baseline, so regressions on earlier cases go unnoticed, and the reviewer's standard drifts. A good answer names these and proposes a versioned dataset with scored, comparable runs.

questions.q: You changed a prompt and five demo questions look better. What do you do before shipping?
questions.a: Run the change against the full stored eval set and compare to the baseline score, per category, with repeated runs or temperature control to separate signal from noise. Look for regressions in cases that were previously passing, then add the demo questions to the dataset. Do not ship on five hand-picked wins.

questions.q: Why is vibe testing a poor release gate?
questions.a: Biased tiny samples, stochastic outputs, no baseline, reviewer drift. A versioned scored set is the gate.

questions.q: You changed a prompt and five demos look better. What before shipping?
questions.a: Run the frozen set, compare to baseline by slice, look for regressions, then add the demos to the set.

questions.q: What does a public chatbot policy failure teach?
questions.a: Fluent answers without a citation or refuse rule become company policy in the user’s eyes. Add that case.

questions.q: What is reviewer drift?
questions.a: Your standard changing with mood and fatigue so today’s “good” is not last Tuesday’s.

deterministic-vs-probabilistic-testing.explain:
## What it is

Traditional software tests are **deterministic**: same input, same output, assert equality. LLM systems are **probabilistic**: the same prompt can yield different wording, and many different outputs can all be correct.

Consequences:
- Exact-match assertions only work for constrained outputs (a label, JSON field, a number).
- For free text you assert **properties** (contains the refund policy, under 120 words, valid JSON, no PII) or score with a rubric or judge.
- Results are **statistical**: report pass rate over N cases, often with repeated runs, and compare with a tolerance rather than expecting 100%.

Example: a classifier at temperature 0 can be tested with equality, but a summariser needs checks like "mentions all three action items" and a threshold such as 90% of cases passing.

Trap: setting temperature to 0 does not guarantee determinism across providers, batching or model updates. Treat flakiness as a measurement problem: more samples, fixed seeds where supported, and thresholds with margin.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Software tests assert equality. LLM tests usually cannot. Many wordings are correct; sampling changes them. You assert properties or scores and gate on a pass rate with tolerance.

Temperature 0 is not determinism across providers or versions.

## How it works + one small example

Constrained output (label, JSON field): equality or schema. Free text: required facts, length, format, safety, or a rubric. Repeat n times if variance is high. Report 90% of cases passing, not “the test passed.”

Pin model versions. Treat flakes as measurement: more samples or a wider tolerance, not a retry-until-green.

## Failure modes

1. **Exact-match on summaries.**

2. **Assuming temperature 0 is enough.**

3. **Retrying CI until green without changing the assertion.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I test properties and pass rates, not string equality, on free text. Temperature 0 reduces noise; it does not make a unit test deterministic.

## A concrete walk-through

A summary test compared to one golden string and failed 1/10 in CI. You switch to “contains three action items, <120 words” and a 90% threshold. The flake ends; a real regression still fails.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about snapshots. Say: snapshots of properties, not of full prose.

## What I would measure

Flake rate, assertion type mix, pass-rate vs single-run gates.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Flake rate, assertion type mix, pass-rate vs single-run gates. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Equality only for constrained outputs. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: I test properties and pass rates, not string equality, on free text. Temperature 0 reduces noise; it does not make a unit test deterministic. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about snapshots. Say: snapshots of properties, not of full prose. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Free text: properties or rubrics.
keyPoints: Gate on pass rates with tolerance.
Free-text LLM output needs property checks or rubric scoring, not equality
Report pass rates with tolerances, not a single pass/fail

questions.q: Why can't you simply assert equality on LLM summaries in a unit test?
questions.a: Many different wordings are equally correct and sampling changes them run to run, so equality produces false failures. Instead assert properties (required facts present, length, format, safety) or score with a rubric or judge, and gate on an aggregate pass rate.

questions.q: A test passes locally but fails 1 in 10 runs in CI with temperature 0. How do you handle it?
questions.a: Recognise that provider-side nondeterminism and model updates still cause variance. Run each case multiple times, measure the pass rate, set a threshold with margin, pin model versions, and make assertions property-based rather than exact. Do not just retry until green.

questions.q: Why can't you simply assert equality on LLM summaries?
questions.a: Many correct wordings exist and sampling changes them. Assert properties or a rubric and gate on a pass rate.

questions.q: A test passes locally but fails 1 in 10 in CI at temperature 0. What do you do?
questions.a: Treat it as variance. Repeat, set a threshold, pin versions, use property checks. Do not retry until green.

questions.q: When is equality OK?
questions.a: Labels, enums, schema-valid JSON fields, exact numbers you required.

questions.q: What does a 90% pass-rate gate mean?
questions.a: At least 90% of cases meet the property; you accept some sampling noise rather than demanding 100% identical strings.

model-evals-vs-application-evals.explain:
## What it is

**Model evals** ask how good a general-purpose model is: benchmarks like reasoning, coding or knowledge tests, usually run by labs or leaderboards. **Application evals** ask whether *your* system, with your prompts, retrieval, tools and users, does the job.

Differences:
- Model evals use public, generic tasks; application evals use your data, your failure modes and your definition of good.
- A model that tops a leaderboard can still fail your task if your prompt, context or output format is different.
- Application evals cover the whole pipeline: retrieval quality, tool use, formatting, safety, latency and cost.

Use model evals to **shortlist** candidates and application evals to **decide** and to guard releases. Interview angle: when asked how you chose a model, answer that benchmarks narrowed the field and a custom eval on a representative sample made the call.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Model evals (MMLU, coding benches) ask how good a general model is. Application evals ask whether your prompt, retrieval, tools and format work on your data. Leaderboard rank does not transfer.

Shortlist with model evals; decide with application evals.

## How it works + one small example

Use a leaderboard to pick 3–5 candidates that fit context, cost and capability. Run your 80-case set under the same prompts. Pick with quality/latency/cost. Re-run on every prompt or model change.

A coding champ that cannot emit your JSON is a failed application eval.

## Failure modes

1. **Swapping models because of a tweeted rank.**

2. **No application set, so you cannot decide.**

3. **Changing the prompt when you “compare” models.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Model evals shortlist. Application evals decide. I never swap on a leaderboard rank alone.

## A concrete walk-through

A new model leads a coding board. Your extract set drops 5 points on JSON. You do not swap. The write-up has both numbers.

## Interview follow-up

They ask if you ignore benches. No — you use them to not waste time on hopeless models.

## What I would measure

Candidates shortlisted vs decided, rank-only swaps (0).

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Candidates shortlisted vs decided, rank-only swaps (0). That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Model evals: generic public tasks. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: Model evals shortlist. Application evals decide. I never swap on a leaderboard rank alone. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask if you ignore benches. No — you use them to not waste time on hopeless models. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Application evals: your pipeline and data.
keyPoints: Application evals: your pipeline and data.
Re-run application evals on every change.
Model evals are generic; application evals use your task and data
Leaderboard rank does not predict your pipeline's quality

questions.q: What is the difference between a model eval and an application eval?
questions.a: A model eval measures general capability on public tasks; an application eval measures whether your specific system (prompt, retrieval, tools, format, safety) meets your requirements on your data. The first helps choose candidates, the second is what you release against.

questions.q: A new model leads a coding leaderboard. Your team wants to swap it in immediately. What should you do?
questions.a: Run your own application eval set on both models under the same prompts and settings, compare quality, latency and cost, and check regressions by category. Leaderboards test different tasks and prompt formats, so rank alone does not transfer.

questions.q: A new model leads a coding leaderboard. Your team wants to swap now. What do you do?
questions.a: Run your application set on both under the same prompts. Compare quality, latency, cost, and slice regressions.

questions.q: Why might a leaderboard winner fail you?
questions.a: Different prompts, formats, retrieval and data. Rank is not your pipeline.

questions.q: When is a model eval enough?
questions.a: Never to ship. Only to drop candidates you will not bother testing.

the-end-to-end-evaluation-workflow.explain:
## What it is

A practical eval workflow is a loop, not a one-off:

1. **Define behaviours** you care about (correctness, groundedness, tone, safety) and failure modes.
2. **Collect a dataset**: real or realistic inputs, with expected outputs or criteria where needed.
3. **Choose metrics and methods**: programmatic checks, human review, LLM-as-a-judge.
4. **Run the system** and record outputs, traces, latency and cost.
5. **Score and analyse**: aggregate, slice by category, read failures.
6. **Improve** prompt, retrieval, model or tools, then rerun and compare to the baseline.
7. **Gate and monitor**: run in CI before release, sample production traffic after, and feed new failures back into the dataset.

The key habit is error analysis: reading real failures to decide what to measure next. Without it, teams optimise metrics that do not match user pain.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Eval is a loop: define behaviours, collect a dataset, pick methods, run, score, analyse, improve, gate, monitor, feed failures back. Skipping error analysis is how green metrics hide angry users.

Interviews: walk the loop and linger on error analysis.

## How it works + one small example

Write the behaviours (correct, grounded, safe). Collect 50 real-ish cases. Pick programmatic + judge + some human. Run and store traces. Slice by intent. Read 20 failures. Change one thing. Diff the baseline. CI on the core set. Sample prod.

The artefact is the living dataset, not a one-off spreadsheet.

## Failure modes

1. **Metrics without reading failures.**

2. **A dataset that never grows.**

3. **No baseline so “improve” is a vibe.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Define, dataset, methods, run, analyse, improve, gate, monitor. Error analysis decides the next metric. The set is a living artefact.

## A concrete walk-through

Users hate missing citations. Your metrics were green on fluency. You add a citation check, 30 new cases from tickets, and a gate. The next prompt change cannot drop citations silently.

## Interview follow-up

They ask where to start. Thirty cases, one checker, run on every prompt change.

## What I would measure

Failures read per week, cases added from prod, gates that actually blocked.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Failures read per week, cases added from prod, gates that actually blocked. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: The loop: define → data → methods → run → analyse → improve → gate → monitor. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: Define, dataset, methods, run, analyse, improve, gate, monitor. Error analysis decides the next metric. The set is a living artefact. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask where to start. Thirty cases, one checker, run on every prompt change. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Error analysis is the steering wheel.
keyPoints: The loop: define → data → methods → run → analyse → improve → gate → monitor.
Error analysis is the steering wheel.
Define behaviours, dataset, metrics, run, analyse, improve, gate
Error analysis of real failures drives what to measure

questions.q: Walk through the end-to-end evaluation workflow.
questions.a: Define behaviours and failure modes, build a dataset, pick methods (programmatic, human, judge), run the system and store outputs, score and slice results, read failures, change the system, rerun against a baseline, then gate releases in CI and monitor production feeding failures back into the dataset.

questions.q: Your metrics are green but users complain. Which workflow step has likely been skipped?
questions.a: Error analysis and dataset realism: the dataset or metrics do not reflect real user failures. Sample production traces, categorise failures, add those cases and criteria to the eval set, and make sure the metrics measure what users actually care about.

questions.q: Metrics are green but users complain. Which step was skipped?
questions.a: Error analysis and dataset realism. Sample prod, add those cases and criteria.

questions.q: What is the smallest honest start?
questions.a: Thirty cases, expected shape, one checker, run on every prompt change.

questions.q: What makes the dataset “living”?
questions.a: Versioned adds from prod failures, with a frozen core so trends stay comparable.

unit-slice-and-end-to-end-evals.explain:
## What it is

**Test retrieval, generation and the product separately.** Unit (or component) evals score one piece: retriever recall, generator faithfulness on gold context. Slice evals score a subset (refunds, Hindi, long docs). End-to-end scores the user-visible answer.

You need all three or you cannot localise a drop.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the architecture of an eval suite. Interviewers ask why e2e alone is slow to debug. On the job a 4-point e2e drop that is actually retrieval is a week wasted if you only have e2e.

## How it works + one small example

Same cases, three views. Retriever: gold chunk ids. Generator: gold context, score faithfulness. E2E: full pipeline. Slices: tag cases. A dashboard that cannot filter is a vanity chart.

## Failure modes

1. **Only e2e.**

2. **Component wins that hide a bad interaction.**

3. **Slices so small they are noise.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I test retrieval, generation and the product separately, and I slice. E2E without components cannot localise; components without e2e miss interactions.

## A concrete walk-through

E2E drops 5. Retriever recall is flat; generator on gold is down. You fix the prompt, not the index. Time-to-cause is an hour, not a week.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about cost. Component sets can be cheaper and run on every PR; e2e nightly.

## What I would measure

Time-to-localise a drop, slice coverage, interaction bugs only e2e caught.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Time-to-localise a drop, slice coverage, interaction bugs only e2e caught. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Component, slice and e2e are all required. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: I test retrieval, generation and the product separately, and I slice. E2E without components cannot localise; components without e2e miss interactions. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about cost. Component sets can be cheaper and run on every PR; e2e nightly. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Same cases, different views.

## What would change my mind

This is the architecture of an eval suite. Interviewers ask why e2e alone is slow to debug. On the job a 4-point e2e drop that is actually retrieval is a week wasted if you only have e2e. I change the design when a held-out slice moves, not when a demo is prettier. A third point that would force a redesign is: E2E localises poorly alone. One counter-example that lives in the golden set beats a week of vibe testing.
keyPoints: Component, slice and e2e are all required.
Tier: cheap components on PR, e2e nightly.

questions.q: Why test retrieval, generation and the product separately?
questions.a: To localise a drop: recall vs faithfulness vs user-visible quality. E2E alone cannot say which broke.

questions.q: E2E dropped. What do you run next?
questions.a: Component evals on the same cases — retriever and generator — plus slices.

questions.q: A component is green and e2e is red. What is that?
questions.a: An interaction failure (assembly, truncation, order). Debug the pipeline.

questions.q: What is a slice eval?
questions.a: The same metrics on a tagged subset: intent, language, length, a known hard class.

questions.q: How do you cost-control the suite?
questions.a: Components on PRs, full e2e nightly, slices in both if they are cheap enough.

vibe-testing-as-a-prototype-only.explain:
## What it is

**Pair vibe testing with a frozen set the moment a second person uses the app.** That is the operating rule. One builder clicking around is fine. The second person is a user; their cases go into a file with a date.

If you wait for “later,” you will ship on vibes.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the practical closer to the vibe-testing topic. Interviews love a trigger: second user, first ticket, first prompt change — freeze.

## How it works + one small example

Trigger events: second account, first external ticket, first A/B, first model bump. Action: 20 cases in git, a one-command run, a baseline number in the README.

Vibe can continue beside the set. It just cannot be the gate.

## Failure modes

1. **Waiting for 1,000 cases before any set.**

2. **A set that lives in one person’s notes app.**

3. **Second user arrived and nobody froze.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Vibe until the second person shows up. Then a frozen set in git is the gate. Vibe may continue; it does not ship.

## A concrete walk-through

A teammate tries the bot and finds a refund miss. You add 15 of their prompts that day. The next prompt tweak is gated. That is the culture.

## Interview follow-up

They ask how many cases. Start 20–30. Grow from failures. Do not wait for perfect.

## What I would measure

Time from second user to first frozen set, cases in git, vibe-only ships after that (0).

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Time from second user to first frozen set, cases in git, vibe-only ships after that (0). That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Second user is the trigger to freeze. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: Vibe until the second person shows up. Then a frozen set in git is the gate. Vibe may continue; it does not ship. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask how many cases. Start 20–30. Grow from failures. Do not wait for perfect. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: 20–30 cases in git beat a perfect plan.

## What would change my mind

This is the practical closer to the vibe-testing topic. Interviews love a trigger: second user, first ticket, first prompt change — freeze. I change the design when a held-out slice moves, not when a demo is prettier. A third point that would force a redesign is: Vibe may continue; it is not the gate. One counter-example that lives in the golden set beats a week of vibe testing.

## How this shows up in a log

In a real trace I want to see the decision, the evidence, and the stop. A reviewer should be able to replay this walk-through from the log: A teammate tries the bot and finds a refund miss. You add 15 of their prompts that day. The next prompt tweak is gated. That is the culture. If the log cannot support that story, the feature is not observable yet. I also want the cheap how-it-works sketch nearby so a new teammate can implement the same check: Trigger events: second account, first external ticket, first A/B, first model bump. Action: 20 cases in git, a one-command run, a baseline number in the README. Vibe can continue beside the set. It just cannot be the gate.
keyPoints: Second user is the trigger to freeze.
20–30 cases in git beat a perfect plan.
Vibe may continue; it is not the gate.

questions.q: When must vibe testing stop being the gate?
questions.a: The moment a second person uses the app — freeze a set that day.

questions.q: What is the smallest frozen set?
questions.a: About 20–30 cases in git with a one-command run and a baseline number.

questions.q: May you still vibe after that?
questions.a: Yes, for exploration. Not for the ship decision.

questions.q: The set lives in a Slack thread. Problem?
questions.a: It is not versioned or runnable. Put it in git.

questions.q: Why not wait for a huge set?
questions.a: You will ship on vibes while you wait. Grow from failures.

interview.explain:
## What it is

The interview one-liner for your first eval: **30 cases, expected shape, one judge or checker, run on every prompt change.** Say it, then add “baseline stored, slice if I can, error analysis weekly.”

Do not start with a vendor platform.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the Level 7 opener. Juniors describe RAGAS. Seniors describe a file and a command. On the job this is also how you start Monday.

## How it works + one small example

Thirty real or realistic inputs. Expected: a label, a JSON schema, a must-include list, or a 1–5 rubric. Checker: code first, judge if you must. `make eval` on every prompt PR. Paste the number in the PR.

Have a 60-second story of a change the set blocked.

## Failure modes

1. **Leading with a platform logo.**

2. **30 synthetic twins of one prompt.**

3. **A set you do not run on every change.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

My first eval is 30 cases, an expected shape, one checker, run on every prompt change. The baseline lives next to the prompt.

## A concrete walk-through

In a screen you open `eval/cases.json` and `make eval`. A prompt PR shows −4 on refunds. That is the interview.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about judges. You say you calibrate or you prefer code when you can.

## What I would measure

Whether you can run the set in one command in the interview.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Whether you can run the set in one command in the interview. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: 30 cases, expected shape, one checker. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: My first eval is 30 cases, an expected shape, one checker, run on every prompt change. The baseline lives next to the prompt. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about judges. You say you calibrate or you prefer code when you can. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Run on every prompt change.

## What would change my mind

This is the Level 7 opener. Juniors describe RAGAS. Seniors describe a file and a command. On the job this is also how you start Monday. I change the design when a held-out slice moves, not when a demo is prettier. A third point that would force a redesign is: Code before a judge. One counter-example that lives in the golden set beats a week of vibe testing.

## How this shows up in a log

In a real trace I want to see the decision, the evidence, and the stop. A reviewer should be able to replay this walk-through from the log: In a screen you open `eval/cases.json` and `make eval`. A prompt PR shows −4 on refunds. That is the interview. If the log cannot support that story, the feature is not observable yet. I also want the cheap how-it-works sketch nearby so a new teammate can implement the same check: Thirty real or realistic inputs. Expected: a label, a JSON schema, a must-include list, or a 1–5 rubric. Checker: code first, judge if you must. `make eval` on every prompt PR. Paste the number in the PR. Have a 60-second story of a change the set blocked.
keyPoints: Have a story the set blocked.

questions.q: What is the interview one-liner for a first eval?
questions.a: 30 cases, expected shape, one judge or checker, run on every prompt change.

questions.q: What is “expected shape”?
questions.a: A label, schema, must-include list, or a short rubric — something a checker can score.

questions.q: When do you introduce a vendor eval platform?
questions.a: After the file and the command exist. The platform is optional plumbing.

questions.q: 30 near-duplicate cases — is that a first eval?
questions.a: No. Diversity matters more than count. Include hard and recent misses.

questions.q: Where does the baseline live?
questions.a: Next to the prompt, in git, shown on the PR.

who-owns-the-golden-set.explain:
## What it is

**Product plus engineering; it is a living artefact, not a data-science side quest.** Product owns which behaviours matter and which failures hurt. Engineering owns format, runners, gates. Together they add cases from tickets. A set owned only by an ML person dies when they are busy.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Ownership is why sets rot. Interviews: name two roles. On the job, put the path in the team charter.

## How it works + one small example

RACI: product = criteria and priority slices; eng = schema, CI, PII hygiene; both = weekly add-from-tickets. The set has a README with owners.

Legal/privacy reviews PII. Nobody “owns the vibes.”

## Failure modes

1. **DS-only ownership.**

2. **Product dumps screenshots into a folder with no schema.**

3. **No owner so nobody updates after launch.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

The golden set is a product+engineering artefact. I can name the owners. It is not a side quest and it does not live in one notebook.

## A concrete walk-through

You add `CODEOWNERS` on `eval/`. A ticket cannot close without a case if it was a model miss. Six months later the set still matches the product.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about data science. They contribute judges and analysis; they do not disappear with the only copy.

## What I would measure

Cases added per month, owner response time, orphan sets.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Cases added per month, owner response time, orphan sets. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Product + engineering own the set. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: The golden set is a product+engineering artefact. I can name the owners. It is not a side quest and it does not live in one notebook. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about data science. They contribute judges and analysis; they do not disappear with the only copy. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Product: behaviours and slices.

## What would change my mind

Ownership is why sets rot. Interviews: name two roles. On the job, put the path in the team charter. I change the design when a held-out slice moves, not when a demo is prettier. A third point that would force a redesign is: Eng: schema, CI, PII. One counter-example that lives in the golden set beats a week of vibe testing.

## How this shows up in a log

In a real trace I want to see the decision, the evidence, and the stop. A reviewer should be able to replay this walk-through from the log: You add `CODEOWNERS` on `eval/`. A ticket cannot close without a case if it was a model miss. Six months later the set still matches the product. If the log cannot support that story, the feature is not observable yet. I also want the cheap how-it-works sketch nearby so a new teammate can implement the same check: RACI: product = criteria and priority slices; eng = schema, CI, PII hygiene; both = weekly add-from-tickets. The set has a README with owners. Legal/privacy reviews PII. Nobody “owns the vibes.”

questions.q: Who owns the golden set?
questions.a: Product and engineering together. It is a living artefact, not a data-science side quest.

questions.q: What does product own versus eng?
questions.a: Product: which behaviours and slices matter. Eng: format, runner, gates, PII hygiene. Both add cases.

questions.q: The only copy is in an intern’s Colab. Risk?
questions.a: The set dies when they leave and nobody can run the gate.

questions.q: Must every ticket become a case?
questions.a: Every model-miss ticket should be considered. Noise tickets need not.

questions.q: Where is ownership written?
questions.a: README and CODEOWNERS on the eval path.

programmatic-human-llm-as-a-judge.explain:
## What it is

Three ways to score an output:

- **Programmatic**: code checks such as exact match, regex, JSON schema validity, unit tests for generated code, length limits. Cheap, fast, deterministic, but only for things you can express as rules.
- **Human**: experts or users rate outputs. Highest validity for nuance (tone, usefulness), but slow, costly and subject to inter-rater disagreement.
- **LLM-as-a-Judge**: a model scores outputs against a rubric. Scales to thousands of cases and handles open-ended text, but has biases (favours longer answers, its own style, first position) and must be **calibrated against human labels**.

Typical stack: programmatic checks first as hard gates, a judge for subjective criteria at scale, and periodic human review to audit the judge. Use a different or stronger model as judge where possible and give it narrow, binary or low-cardinality rubrics rather than vague 1-10 scores.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Three execution mechanisms: programmatic (code, schema, tests), human (labels, review), LLM-as-judge (a model scores with a rubric). Pick the cheapest that matches the behaviour. Interviews: programmatic first.

## How it works + one small example

JSON valid? Code. Code works? Tests. Tone? Rubric + humans then a judge you calibrated. Do not judge what a regex can do.

A judge is another system: version it, calibrate it, budget it.

## Failure modes

1. **Judge for schema validity.**

2. **Humans on every batch with no rubric.**

3. **Uncalibrated judge as the only gate.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Programmatic first, humans for new failure types, judges for scale after calibration. I do not pay a model to check JSON.

## A concrete walk-through

You replace a fluency judge with a schema check and a must-include list. Cost drops 80%; a real tone issue still goes to a calibrated judge on a sample.

## Interview follow-up

They ask if judges replace humans. No. They extend a calibrated rubric.

## What I would measure

Share of checks that are code vs judge vs human, judge-human agreement.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Share of checks that are code vs judge vs human, judge-human agreement. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Three mechanisms: code, human, judge. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: Programmatic first, humans for new failure types, judges for scale after calibration. I do not pay a model to check JSON. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask if judges replace humans. No. They extend a calibrated rubric. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Code first.
keyPoints: Judges scale a rubric after calibration.
A judge is a versioned system.
Do not judge what code can decide.
Programmatic is cheap and deterministic but limited to rule-expressible checks
Human is most valid but slow and inconsistent

questions.q: Compare programmatic, human and LLM-judge evaluation.
questions.a: Programmatic checks are cheap, deterministic and good for format or exact facts; humans are the most valid for nuance but slow, costly and variable; LLM judges scale to open-ended text but carry biases and need calibration with human labels. A good answer combines them in layers.

questions.q: Your LLM judge scores long answers higher regardless of quality. How do you detect and mitigate it?
questions.a: Check correlation of judge score with length and compare against human labels on a sample. Mitigate with a rubric that penalises padding, length-controlled comparisons, pairwise swaps of position, and explicit instructions plus calibration examples.

questions.q: Which signal is cheapest for valid JSON with required fields?
questions.a: Schema validation in code.

questions.q: When do you use a human?
questions.a: To define new failure types and to calibrate a judge — not to tick 1,500 obvious format checks.

questions.q: What must you do before trusting a judge?
questions.a: Spot-check against humans and version the judge prompt.

questions.q: A judge scores schema. What do you do?
questions.a: Delete it. Use a validator.

reference-based-vs-reference-free.explain:
## What it is

**Reference-based** evaluation compares the output to a known good answer (ground truth): exact match, F1, embedding similarity, or a judge asked "is this equivalent to the reference?". It needs labelled data but is anchored and consistent.

**Reference-free** evaluation judges the output on its own against criteria or against the input/context: is it faithful to the retrieved context, is it fluent, safe, well-formatted, on-topic? No ground truth is needed, so it works on live traffic.

Trade-offs:
- Reference-based is better for tasks with a correct answer (extraction, QA, classification), but penalises valid alternative phrasings.
- Reference-free scales to production but is only as good as the criteria or judge, and cannot tell whether a confident answer is actually correct.

Common pattern: reference-based offline on the golden set, reference-free online for monitoring.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Reference-based scores against a gold answer (exact, F1, entailment). Reference-free scores against criteria or context (faithfulness to retrieved text, safety) with no gold string. Live traffic usually has no gold.

Use both: gold where you have it; criteria online.

## How it works + one small example

Offline: a labelled set with references for correctness. Online: faithfulness, toxicity, format — no gold needed. Do not force exact match on paraphrases; use semantic equivalence or multiple references.

## Failure modes

1. **Exact match on valid paraphrases.**

2. **No reference-free metrics online so you are blind.**

3. **A “gold” written by the model under test.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

References when I have them; criteria when I do not. I do not punish valid paraphrase with exact match, and I do not let the candidate write the gold.

## A concrete walk-through

A correct paraphrase scored 0 on BLEU-ish overlap. You switch to a claim checklist. The metric stops lying.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about embeddings as similarity. Use carefully; they can reward fluent off-topic text.

## What I would measure

False fails on paraphrase, online coverage with reference-free metrics.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: False fails on paraphrase, online coverage with reference-free metrics. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Reference-based needs gold. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: References when I have them; criteria when I do not. I do not punish valid paraphrase with exact match, and I do not let the candidate write the gold. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about embeddings as similarity. Use carefully; they can reward fluent off-topic text. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Reference-free uses criteria or context.
keyPoints: The candidate must not write the gold.
Reference-based needs ground truth and is anchored
Reference-free judges against criteria or context and works on live traffic

questions.q: When would you choose reference-free evaluation?
questions.a: When there is no single correct answer or no labels exist, such as monitoring production traffic or judging tone and faithfulness to context. It checks the output against criteria or the input, but cannot verify factual correctness beyond the provided context.

questions.q: Why can reference-based scoring undercount a correct answer?
questions.a: If it relies on string overlap or embedding similarity to a single reference, a valid answer phrased differently scores low. Use semantic or judge-based equivalence, multiple references, or constrained outputs to reduce this.

questions.q: You monitor live traffic with no ground truth. Which approach fits?
questions.a: Reference-free criteria such as faithfulness to context and safety.

questions.q: A correct paraphrase is scored wrong. Fix?
questions.a: Semantic equivalence, multiple references, or a claim checklist — not exact match.

questions.q: Why not let the candidate model write the gold?
questions.a: It will favour its own style and hide its failures.

questions.q: When is reference-based required?
questions.a: When you must know factual correctness against a known answer, not just faithfulness to retrieved text.

when-a-golden-dataset-is-required.explain:
## What it is

A **golden dataset** is a curated set of inputs with trusted expected outputs or labels. It is required when you need **comparable, repeatable numbers**: regression testing, comparing models or prompts, measuring retrieval recall, or calibrating an LLM judge.

You can skip it for early exploration, for purely reference-free monitoring, and for rule-checkable properties such as valid JSON that need no labels.

What makes one good: representative of real traffic, covers edge cases and known failures, has unambiguous labels agreed by reviewers, is versioned, and is not leaked into prompts or fine-tuning data. Size matters less than coverage; a few dozen well-chosen cases per category beats thousands of near-duplicates. Start small, then grow it from production failures.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

A golden set (inputs + expected answers or criteria) is required when you compare versions, gate releases, or measure correctness. Pure judge-on-the-fly cannot give you a stable baseline if the judge or the traffic mix moves.

You can judge without gold for monitoring; you cannot do apples-to-apples without a frozen set.

## How it works + one small example

Build gold for: model/prompt bake-offs, CI gates, factual tasks (SQL, rates). Skip gold for: exploratory UX, one-off red-teams (use notes). Mix: a frozen core plus a growing pool.

Size: enough to slice. 30 is a start; 200 with tags is a suite.

## Failure modes

1. **Gating on a live judge with no frozen cases.**

2. **A 1,500-case set of duplicates.**

3. **Gold that is stale relative to the product.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I need a golden set to compare and to gate. A live judge without frozen cases cannot tell me if I got better. Diversity beats raw count.

## A concrete walk-through

You try to compare two prompts on today’s traffic. The mix shifted. You cannot tell. You go back to a 120-case gold core and the comparison is real.

## Interview follow-up

They ask if gold must include full answers. Criteria can be enough if they are specific.

## What I would measure

Frozen-core size, duplicate rate, age of cases vs product.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Frozen-core size, duplicate rate, age of cases vs product. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Gold is required to compare and to gate. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: I need a golden set to compare and to gate. A live judge without frozen cases cannot tell me if I got better. Diversity beats raw count. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask if gold must include full answers. Criteria can be enough if they are specific. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Live judges monitor; they do not replace a frozen core.
keyPoints: Gold is required to compare and to gate.
Live judges monitor; they do not replace a frozen core.
Criteria can stand in for full answers.
Keep a frozen core as the product changes.
Do not gold-label the candidate’s own outputs as truth.
Needed for repeatable comparison, regression tests and judge calibration
Quality means representativeness, edge cases, clear labels and versioning

questions.q: When is a golden dataset required and when can you do without?
questions.a: Required for regression tests, model or prompt comparison, retrieval metrics and judge calibration, because you need stable labelled expectations. Not strictly needed for exploration, rule-based property checks, or reference-free production monitoring.

questions.q: A teammate built 2,000 golden cases by generating variations of 20 prompts. Is that good?
questions.a: Probably not: size hides low diversity. Near-duplicates inflate scores and miss real distribution and edge cases. Audit coverage by category, sample real traffic, dedupe, and add hard cases and known failures.

questions.q: When is a Golden Dataset required versus LLM judgment only?
questions.a: Required for bake-offs, CI gates and correctness. Judgment-only can monitor live traffic but cannot give a stable comparison.

questions.q: A 1,500-case set scores 98% but users fail. Likely cause?
questions.a: Near-duplicates and missing real edges. Coverage beats count.

questions.q: Can criteria replace full gold answers?
questions.a: Yes, if they are specific (must include X, must not promise Y).

questions.q: Why keep a frozen core as the set grows?
questions.a: So trend lines are comparable and you cannot tune against the whole moving set.

matching-method-to-behaviour.explain:
## What it is

Pick the evaluation method from the **behaviour** you want to verify, not from what tooling is handy.

- Structured output, schema, length, banned words: **programmatic** checks.
- Extraction or classification with one right answer: **reference-based** exact or F1.
- Code generation: **execute tests**.
- Faithfulness to retrieved context, tone, helpfulness, completeness: **LLM judge** with a rubric.
- Safety nuance, brand voice, high-stakes domain: **human review**, at least to calibrate.
- Tool use and multi-step agents: check the **trajectory** and tool calls, not just the final text.

Prefer the cheapest method that is valid for the behaviour, and layer them. The common mistake is using a judge for something a regex settles, which adds cost and noise, or using exact match for open-ended text.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Match the method to the behaviour: deterministic → code; semantic → overlap/entailment/judge; subjective → rubric + human/judge; operational → systems metrics. A mismatch is wasted spend or a lying number.

## How it works + one small example

Write the behaviour first. “Valid JSON” is deterministic. “Same meaning as gold” is semantic. “Polite” is subjective. “p95 < 2s” is operational. Then pick.

A table in the eval README: behaviour → method → owner.

## Failure modes

1. **Judge on latency.**

2. **BLEU on a chatbot’s empathy.**

3. **No operational metrics at all.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I match method to behaviour: code for deterministic, semantic checks for meaning, rubric for taste, systems metrics for ops. Mismatches lie.

## A concrete walk-through

A team judged “is JSON valid?” You replace it with a parser. They judged latency too. You move that to p95 in the same dashboard.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about hybrid. Yes: code AND a rubric on the same case.

## What I would measure

Mismatched methods retired, table completeness.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Mismatched methods retired, table completeness. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Behaviour first, method second. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: I match method to behaviour: code for deterministic, semantic checks for meaning, rubric for taste, systems metrics for ops. Mismatches lie. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about hybrid. Yes: code AND a rubric on the same case. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Deterministic → code.

## What would change my mind

Match the method to the behaviour: deterministic → code; semantic → overlap/entailment/judge; subjective → rubric + human/judge; operational → systems metrics. A mismatch is wasted spend or a lying number. I change the design when a held-out slice moves, not when a demo is prettier. A third point that would force a redesign is: Semantic → entailment/judge/overlap. One counter-example that lives in the golden set beats a week of vibe testing.
keyPoints: Write the mapping in the README.
Choose the method per behaviour, cheapest valid option first
Code runs tests; schema uses validators; subjective traits use judge plus human audit

questions.q: Which method would you use to evaluate a JSON extraction task, and which for tone?
questions.a: JSON extraction: programmatic schema validation plus reference-based field comparison. Tone: an LLM judge with a rubric, calibrated by human review, because it is subjective and not rule-expressible.

questions.q: Why is using an LLM judge for every check a mistake?
questions.a: It adds cost, latency and judge noise for checks that deterministic code settles reliably, such as format or banned strings. Use programmatic checks first, reserve judges for subjective criteria.

questions.q: How do you choose an evaluation method?
questions.a: By the behaviour: deterministic, semantic, subjective or operational — then the cheapest fitting method.

questions.q: Code generation should most reliably be evaluated by?
questions.a: Executing unit tests against the generated code.

questions.q: A judge scores p95 latency. Verdict?
questions.a: Wrong method. Use system metrics.

questions.q: Can one case use two methods?
questions.a: Yes. Schema in code and a tone rubric on the same output.

llm-as-judge-calibration.explain:
## What it is

**Spot-check the judge against humans before you trust the score.** Calibration is agreement (and disagreement analysis) on a labelled sample. An uncalibrated judge is a second stochastic system you happened to treat as truth.

Re-calibrate when you change the judge prompt, the model, or the product.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the interview follow-up to “we use a judge.” They want kappa or at least a confusion table, and a story of a bias you found (length, position, verbosity).

## How it works + one small example

Label 100 cases with two humans. Run the judge. Report agreement, slices where it fails. Fix the rubric. Freeze the judge version. Re-score the baseline when the judge changes so you do not mistake judge drift for product drift.

## Failure modes

1. **Never comparing to humans.**

2. **Changing the judge and celebrating a +8.**

3. **One human labeler as “truth” with no overlap.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I calibrate the judge on a human sample, I version it, and I re-score the baseline when it changes. An uncalibrated score is not a gate.

## A concrete walk-through

The judge loved long answers. Humans did not. You add a length-neutral rubric. Agreement rises; the product stops padding.

## Interview follow-up

They ask for a number. Pair agreement and a slice table beat a single accuracy.

## What I would measure

Judge-human agreement, judge-version diffs on frozen traces.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Judge-human agreement, judge-version diffs on frozen traces. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Calibrate against humans before gating. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: I calibrate the judge on a human sample, I version it, and I re-score the baseline when it changes. An uncalibrated score is not a gate. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask for a number. Pair agreement and a slice table beat a single accuracy. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Use two human labelers when you can.

## What would change my mind

This is the interview follow-up to “we use a judge.” They want kappa or at least a confusion table, and a story of a bias you found (length, position, verbosity). I change the design when a held-out slice moves, not when a demo is prettier. A third point that would force a redesign is: Version the judge. One counter-example that lives in the golden set beats a week of vibe testing.

## How this shows up in a log

In a real trace I want to see the decision, the evidence, and the stop. A reviewer should be able to replay this walk-through from the log: The judge loved long answers. Humans did not. You add a length-neutral rubric. Agreement rises; the product stops padding. If the log cannot support that story, the feature is not observable yet. I also want the cheap how-it-works sketch nearby so a new teammate can implement the same check: Label 100 cases with two humans. Run the judge. Report agreement, slices where it fails. Fix the rubric. Freeze the judge version. Re-score the baseline when the judge changes so you do not mistake judge drift for product drift.
keyPoints: Use two human labelers when you can.

questions.q: An LLM judge was never compared to humans. Main risk?
questions.a: Its biases and misalignment go unnoticed, so scores may not mean what you think.

questions.q: The quality dashboard dropped 8 after you changed the judge prompt. First step?
questions.a: Re-score the same traces with old and new judge to separate evaluator drift from product drift.

questions.q: What do you report from calibration?
questions.a: Agreement, a confusion or slice table, and known biases.

questions.q: Why two human labelers?
questions.a: To estimate human noise so you do not expect the judge to exceed it.

questions.q: May an uncalibrated judge still explore?
questions.a: Yes, for triage. Not as a release gate.

exact-match-vs-rubric.explain:
## What it is

**Use code for format; use a rubric for quality.** Exact match (or schema, or unit tests) owns deterministic properties. A rubric owns graded quality (completeness, tone, groundedness). Mixing them — a judge that also “checks JSON” — wastes money and hides format bugs in a 1–5 score.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the method-matching closer. Interviews: two columns. On the job the PR checklist says which is which.

## How it works + one small example

Pipeline: parse/validate first (fail fast). Only valid outputs get a rubric. Report both numbers. A format fail is not a 2/5; it is a 0 on format.

Rubric dimensions are few and defined. “Good” is not a dimension.

## Failure modes

1. **One 1–10 score for everything.**

2. **Exact match on tone.**

3. **Rubric on JSON validity.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Code owns format. A rubric owns quality. I fail-fast on schema, then I score the rest. I do not bury a parse error in a 3/5.

## A concrete walk-through

You split a 1–10 judge into schema-pass % and a 3-dimension rubric. A prompt change that broke JSON is now obvious instead of a mild score dip.

## Interview follow-up

They ask how many rubric dimensions. Three to five; more and judges disagree.

## What I would measure

Format-fail rate separate from quality, judge disagreement by dimension.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Format-fail rate separate from quality, judge disagreement by dimension. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Code for format; rubric for quality. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: Code owns format. A rubric owns quality. I fail-fast on schema, then I score the rest. I do not bury a parse error in a 3/5. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask how many rubric dimensions. Three to five; more and judges disagree. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Fail-fast on schema.

## What would change my mind

This is the method-matching closer. Interviews: two columns. On the job the PR checklist says which is which. I change the design when a held-out slice moves, not when a demo is prettier. A third point that would force a redesign is: Do not bury parse errors in a Likert. One counter-example that lives in the golden set beats a week of vibe testing.

## How this shows up in a log

In a real trace I want to see the decision, the evidence, and the stop. A reviewer should be able to replay this walk-through from the log: You split a 1–10 judge into schema-pass % and a 3-dimension rubric. A prompt change that broke JSON is now obvious instead of a mild score dip. If the log cannot support that story, the feature is not observable yet. I also want the cheap how-it-works sketch nearby so a new teammate can implement the same check: Pipeline: parse/validate first (fail fast). Only valid outputs get a rubric. Report both numbers. A format fail is not a 2/5; it is a 0 on format. Rubric dimensions are few and defined. “Good” is not a dimension.

Do not bury parse errors in a Likert.
Exact match is wrong for tone.

questions.q: When do you use exact-match versus a rubric?
questions.a: Exact-match or schema for format and constrained fields; a rubric for graded quality.

questions.q: A 1–10 score dropped 0.4 when JSON broke. What was wrong?
questions.a: Format was buried in a quality score. Split them; fail-fast on schema.

questions.q: How many rubric dimensions?
questions.a: About three to five, defined. “Good” is not one.

questions.q: May unit tests replace a rubric for code gen?
questions.a: For behaviour, yes. You may still rubric style separately.

questions.q: Why fail-fast on format?
questions.a: So you do not pay a judge and so the dashboard shows the real bug.

interview.explain:
## What it is

The method-picking one-liner: **programmatic first, human for new failure types, judge for scale.** Add: calibrate the judge, match method to behaviour, never judge JSON.

This is the M7.2 interview close.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

They will give you a behaviour and wait. Start with code. Mention humans as taxonomy. Mention judges last, with calibration.

## How it works + one small example

Practice on four behaviours: schema, factual with gold, tone, p95. Your answers should be: parser; reference metric or claim check; rubric+human then judge; timer.

Have a story where you deleted a judge.

## Failure modes

1. **Judge-first answer.**

2. **Forgetting operational metrics.**

3. **No calibration mention.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Programmatic first, humans for new failures, judge for scale after I calibrate. I match method to behaviour and I can name one judge I deleted.

## A concrete walk-through

They say “eval this support bot.” You list format checks, a 40-case gold, a tone rubric sampled to humans, p95, then a judge on the rest. They stop asking.

## Interview follow-up

They push a platform. You say it can run those methods; it does not choose them.

## What I would measure

Whether your last design doc used this order.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Whether your last design doc used this order. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Programmatic first. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: Programmatic first, humans for new failures, judge for scale after I calibrate. I match method to behaviour and I can name one judge I deleted. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They push a platform. You say it can run those methods; it does not choose them. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Humans for new failure types.

## What would change my mind

They will give you a behaviour and wait. Start with code. Mention humans as taxonomy. Mention judges last, with calibration. I change the design when a held-out slice moves, not when a demo is prettier. A third point that would force a redesign is: Judge for scale, calibrated. One counter-example that lives in the golden set beats a week of vibe testing.

## How this shows up in a log

In a real trace I want to see the decision, the evidence, and the stop. A reviewer should be able to replay this walk-through from the log: They say “eval this support bot.” You list format checks, a 40-case gold, a tone rubric sampled to humans, p95, then a judge on the rest. They stop asking. If the log cannot support that story, the feature is not observable yet. I also want the cheap how-it-works sketch nearby so a new teammate can implement the same check: Practice on four behaviours: schema, factual with gold, tone, p95. Your answers should be: parser; reference metric or claim check; rubric+human then judge; timer. Have a story where you deleted a judge.

offline-suites-for-pre-release-testing.explain:
## What it is

**Offline evaluation** runs your system on a fixed dataset before release, in a controlled environment. It answers: did this change make things better or worse versus the baseline?

Strengths: repeatable, cheap to iterate, can include adversarial and edge cases, safe because no real users are exposed, and can be wired into CI. You can slice results by category and compare prompts, models or retrieval settings side by side.

Limits: the dataset is only a sample of reality. It goes stale as users change, and it cannot reveal live issues such as real latency under load, traffic you did not anticipate, or drift in upstream APIs.

A good offline suite has a smoke subset (fast, runs on every commit), a full set (nightly or pre-release), and fixed settings (model version, temperature, seeds) so differences reflect your change, not noise.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Offline suites are the frozen cases you run before a release: version compare, experiment, regression. They are the only way to say “this prompt is better” without waiting for users.

They cannot see provider drift after you ship — that is online.

## How it works + one small example

A versioned set, a pinned model id, a command in CI. Compare to the last shipped baseline. Block on a statistically meaningful drop plus any P0 slice.

Keep the suite small enough to run on a PR (smoke) and a full nightly.

## Failure modes

1. **A suite nobody runs.**

2. **Blocking on one flaky case.**

3. **No baseline to compare.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Offline suites gate releases. I run them on a pinned setup, diff the last shipped baseline, and I know they will not see post-ship provider drift.

## A concrete walk-through

A prompt PR drops the refund slice 6 points. CI fails. You fix before users see it. That is the suite earning its keep.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about size. Smoke 20 on PR, 150 nightly.

## What I would measure

PRs blocked, time to run, flakes.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: PRs blocked, time to run, flakes. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Offline = frozen cases before release. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: Offline suites gate releases. I run them on a pinned setup, diff the last shipped baseline, and I know they will not see post-ship provider drift. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about size. Smoke 20 on PR, 150 nightly. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Diff the last shipped baseline.

questions.q: What does an offline eval suite give you that production monitoring does not?
questions.a: Repeatable, controlled comparison against a baseline before any user is exposed, including adversarial and edge cases, and CI gating. Production monitoring shows real traffic but cannot cleanly attribute changes or protect users in advance.

questions.q: Your offline score improved 3 points but you are unsure it is real. What do you check?
questions.a: Run-to-run variance with repeated runs, pinned model and settings, dataset size per slice, and whether gains hold across categories rather than one. Compare with a confidence interval or tolerance before concluding.

questions.q: What is an offline suite for?
questions.a: Pre-release testing, version comparison, experiments and regression — on frozen cases.

questions.a: A hosted model silently updated after release, or a traffic mix shift.

questions.a: Thresholds with tolerance and a smoke/full split.

questions.a: The last shipped prompt/model/config scores on the same set.

post-deployment-production-risks.explain:
## What it is

After release, new risks appear that an offline suite cannot see:

- **Distribution shift**: users ask things you did not sample.
- **Model or provider drift**: hosted models get updated or deprecated; behaviour changes without your code changing.
- **Upstream data change**: the knowledge base, tools or APIs evolve, breaking retrieval or tool calls.
- **Adversarial use**: prompt injection, jailbreaks, abuse.
- **Scale effects**: latency spikes, rate limits, timeouts, cost blowups.
- **Feedback loops**: outputs shape later inputs.

Mitigation is observability: log traces, track system and quality metrics, sample outputs for review, alert on thresholds, and keep rollbacks and pinned versions ready. Interview point: shipping with green offline evals is necessary, not sufficient.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

After you ship: unexpected inputs, systematic failures that emerge at scale, changing user behaviour, data drift, provider model swaps. Offline cannot see these. Online and feedback loops can.

Interviews: name four risks and one control each.

## How it works + one small example

Unexpected inputs: log and sample. Systematic fails: slice dashboards. Behaviour change: track intent mix. Drift: retrieval hit-rate and embedding-space alarms. Provider swap: pin versions or detect id changes.

Each risk has an owner and a page.

## Failure modes

1. **“We have an offline suite” as the whole production story.**

2. **No slice so a 2% toxic intent is invisible.**

3. **Unpinned model ids.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Production adds unexpected inputs, emergent failures, mix shift and drift. I sample, slice, pin versions, and I feed misses back offline.

## A concrete walk-through

A provider silently updates. Your online faithfulness dips. An alert fires. You pin and roll back. Offline would have caught it only next week.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about drift vs mix. Drift is the world changing; mix is who shows up. Both move scores.

## What I would measure

Time-to-detect a silent model change, slice coverage, unpinned ids.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Time-to-detect a silent model change, slice coverage, unpinned ids. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Risks: unexpected inputs, emergent fails, mix shift, drift, provider swaps. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: Production adds unexpected inputs, emergent failures, mix shift and drift. I sample, slice, pin versions, and I feed misses back offline. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about drift vs mix. Drift is the world changing; mix is who shows up. Both move scores. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Controls: sample, slice, pin, alert.
