Distribution shift, provider drift and upstream changes break assumptions
Adversarial use and scale effects only show up live

questions.q: Name production risks that offline evals miss.
questions.a: Distribution shift in user queries, silent model/provider updates, changing upstream data or tools, adversarial inputs, and scale issues such as latency spikes, rate limits and cost. These need tracing, monitoring, alerts and rollback paths.

questions.q: Quality dropped last Tuesday but you deployed nothing. What are likely causes?
questions.a: A provider model update, changed knowledge-base content or tool API, a shift in user query mix, or a degraded dependency. Check model version pins, trace samples before and after, data change logs, and rerun the offline suite on current settings.

questions.q: Name post-deployment risks offline suites miss.
questions.a: Unexpected inputs, emergent systematic failures, changing mix, data drift, silent provider updates.

questions.q: A hosted model updates after release. How do you notice?
questions.a: Online quality metrics and a pinned-id check — not the frozen suite alone.

questions.q: Mix shifted toward a weak slice. Offline is flat. Why?
questions.a: The frozen set does not match today’s mix. Online slices show it.

questions.q: What is the control for unexpected inputs?
questions.a: Log, sample, and add representatives to gold.

system-metrics-vs-quality-metrics.explain:
## What it is

**System metrics** describe how the service runs: latency (p50/p95/p99), time to first token, throughput, error and timeout rates, token usage, cost per request, cache hit rate. They are cheap, objective and always available.

**Quality metrics** describe whether outputs are good: correctness, faithfulness, relevance, completeness, safety, user satisfaction. They are harder, often need a judge or humans, and may be sampled.

Why both: a system can be fast, cheap and wrong, or excellent and unusably slow. Quality can also drop with no system alarm, since a hallucinating model returns HTTP 200. Track them together and look at trade-offs, e.g. whether a cheaper model's cost saving is worth a quality drop on a specific slice. Use percentiles rather than averages for latency.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Latency, tokens, errors are system metrics. Hallucination, relevance, correctness are quality metrics. Green systems can still be wrong. Interviews: both on the same dashboard.

## How it works + one small example

System: p50/p95 latency, error %, tokens, $. Quality: sampled scores (faithfulness, task success). Never let an SLO of 200 OK hide a 30% wrong-answer rate.

Quality is usually sampled and async. System is full-traffic.

## Failure modes

1. **Only system dashboards.**

2. **Inline quality judges on every request (latency+cost).**

3. **Averaging quality without slices.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I show system and quality together. A fast 200 can still be wrong. Quality is sampled; latency is not a quality proxy.

## A concrete walk-through

Ops says the service is healthy. Users complain. You add sampled faithfulness. It is 0.62. Now everyone sees the same fire.

## Interview follow-up

They ask why p95 not mean. Tails hide in means.

## What I would measure

Dashboards that include both, inline-judge rate (should be low).

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Dashboards that include both, inline-judge rate (should be low). That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: System ≠ quality. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: I show system and quality together. A fast 200 can still be wrong. Quality is sampled; latency is not a quality proxy. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask why p95 not mean. Tails hide in means. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Fast 200 can be wrong.

## What would change my mind

Latency, tokens, errors are system metrics. Hallucination, relevance, correctness are quality metrics. Green systems can still be wrong. Interviews: both on the same dashboard. I change the design when a held-out slice moves, not when a demo is prettier. A third point that would force a redesign is: Quality is sampled async. One counter-example that lives in the golden set beats a week of vibe testing.
keyPoints: System metrics: latency, errors, tokens, cost; quality metrics: correctness, faithfulness, safety
Healthy system metrics can hide bad answers

questions.q: Why aren't system metrics enough for LLM apps?
questions.a: A hallucinated or unsafe answer still returns success quickly, so latency and error rates stay green. Quality metrics such as faithfulness and correctness are needed to see output problems.

questions.q: Switching to a cheaper model cut cost 40% with no alerts. What do you verify?
questions.a: Quality metrics by slice on a representative sample (offline and sampled live), plus latency percentiles. Confirm no regression on high-value or hard categories before accepting the saving.

questions.q: Dashboards show low latency and 0% errors, yet answers are wrong. What is missing?
questions.a: Quality metrics on sampled traffic — faithfulness, correctness.

questions.q: Why is p95 latency preferred over mean?
questions.a: Tails hurt users and disappear in the mean.

questions.q: Where should LLM-judge scoring run online?
questions.a: Asynchronously on a sample, not inline before every response.

questions.q: Is token count a quality metric?
questions.a: No. It is a cost/system metric that can correlate either way.

continuous-online-evaluation-pipeline.explain:
## What it is

A **continuous online evaluation pipeline** scores real production traffic as it happens or shortly after.

Steps:
1. **Capture** traces: input, retrieved context, tool calls, output, metadata, versions. Redact PII.
2. **Sample** traffic, because judging everything is costly: random sample plus oversampling of risky or low-feedback cases.
3. **Score** asynchronously with reference-free evaluators (faithfulness, safety, format) and use user signals (thumbs, edits, retries).
4. **Aggregate and alert** on dashboards by slice and version; page on threshold breaches.
5. **Route** failures to human review and the failure backlog.

Keep scoring off the critical path so it adds no user latency. Watch evaluator cost and keep the judge versioned, otherwise a changed judge looks like changed quality.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Online eval is a pipeline: log traces, sample, score, dashboard, alert. It is how you notice drift on Tuesday, not at the next quarterly offline run.

Sampling and async scoring keep it cheap.

## How it works + one small example

Log redacted traces. Sample 5–10% or all of a P0 slice. Score async. Dashboard by slice. Alert on a drop versus a rolling baseline, after you rule out judge changes.

Feed a tagged miss into the gold set automatically as a candidate.

## Failure modes

1. **Logging without sampling policy (cost or gaps).**

2. **Alerting on the judge version bump.**

3. **No PII policy on traces.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Online eval is log, sample, score async, dashboard, alert. I version the scorer so I do not page myself for a rubric change.

## A concrete walk-through

You sample 8%. A slice alert fires at −7. The judge version is unchanged. You roll back a prompt. The candidate gold cases from that hour become tomorrow’s offline adds.

## Interview follow-up

They ask 100% scoring. Only if cheap code checks; judges stay sampled.

## What I would measure

Coverage %, alert precision, time-to-detect a real drop.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Coverage %, alert precision, time-to-detect a real drop. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Log, sample, async score, dashboard, alert. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: Online eval is log, sample, score async, dashboard, alert. I version the scorer so I do not page myself for a rubric change. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask 100% scoring. Only if cheap code checks; judges stay sampled. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Version the scorer.
keyPoints: Log, sample, async score, dashboard, alert.
P0 slices can be 100% if cheap.
Do not page on judge edits.
Capture, sample, score async, aggregate, alert, route failures
Use reference-free evaluators and user signals

questions.q: Describe the stages of a continuous online eval pipeline.
questions.a: Capture redacted traces, sample traffic including risky cases, score asynchronously with reference-free evaluators and user feedback, aggregate by slice and version with alerts, and route failures to review and the dataset backlog.

questions.q: Why should online scoring be asynchronous and sampled?
questions.a: Judging every request inline adds latency and cost to the user path. Async sampled scoring gives statistical visibility cheaply, while oversampling risky traffic keeps important cases covered.

questions.q: What are the stages of an online eval pipeline?
questions.a: Production logging, sampling, scoring, dashboarding and alerting — plus feedback into gold.

questions.q: Why version the online judge?
questions.a: So a rubric change is not mistaken for a product drop.

questions.q: 100% judge coverage — when?
questions.a: Rarely. Prefer 100% on cheap code checks; sample expensive judges.

questions.q: Traces contain emails. What first?
questions.a: Redact and lock access before you scale sampling.

feeding-failures-back-offline.explain:
## What it is

The loop that makes evals improve over time: **production failures become offline test cases**.

Process:
- Detect failures from low judge scores, negative feedback, escalations, safety flags or human review.
- Triage and label them: what should the correct output have been, and what category of failure is it?
- Anonymise and add them to the golden dataset with provenance and version.
- Fix the system, then confirm the new case passes and nothing else regressed.

This turns each incident into a permanent regression test. Watch for dataset contamination (do not tune prompts to memorise cases), privacy (strip PII before storing), and balance, since failures alone skew the set; keep typical successful cases too so the score still reflects normal traffic.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

A production miss that never becomes an offline case will recur. The loop closes when someone (or a job) adds a redacted, labelled case to gold.

This is the “self-improving set” habit at the online/offline boundary.

## How it works + one small example

Triage: is it a model miss? Redact. Label expected criteria. Open a PR to `eval/cases`. Tag the slice. The next CI run includes it.

A thumbs-down with retrieved context is almost a case already — do not throw the context away.

## Failure modes

1. **A graveyard of thumbs-down with no cases.**

2. **Adding raw PII to git.**

3. **Adding 200 near-duplicates from one incident.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Every important prod miss becomes a redacted gold case. Thumbs-down plus context is tomorrow’s offline item. I do not hoard unlabelled traces.

## A concrete walk-through

A week of refund misses becomes 12 cases. The next prompt PR fails until it handles them. Recurrence stops.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about automation. Auto-open a draft case; a human still labels.

## What I would measure

Miss-to-case time, recurrence of the same miss, PII in git.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Miss-to-case time, recurrence of the same miss, PII in git. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Prod misses become gold. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: Every important prod miss becomes a redacted gold case. Thumbs-down plus context is tomorrow’s offline item. I do not hoard unlabelled traces. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about automation. Auto-open a draft case; a human still labels. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Redact first.

## What would change my mind

A production miss that never becomes an offline case will recur. The loop closes when someone (or a job) adds a redacted, labelled case to gold. This is the “self-improving set” habit at the online/offline boundary. I change the design when a held-out slice moves, not when a demo is prettier. A third point that would force a redesign is: Keep retrieved context with the case. One counter-example that lives in the golden set beats a week of vibe testing.

The next CI must include them.

questions.q: How do production failures improve your offline suite?
questions.a: Detected failures are triaged, labelled with the correct behaviour, anonymised and added to the golden dataset, so fixes are verified and the issue cannot silently return. It makes the offline set track real usage.

questions.q: What risk comes from adding only failures to the dataset?
questions.a: The set becomes skewed toward hard cases, making scores look worse than typical traffic and hiding regressions on common cases. Keep a balanced sample of normal traffic and track slices separately.

questions.q: What is the best use of a production failure after triage?

questions.a: Better with the retrieved context and the prompt. Save those fields.

questions.a: A human (often eng+product). A job may draft the file.

questions.q: Why not add every thumbs-down automatically as gold truth?
questions.a: Thumbs are noisy. Triage first or you poison the set.

online-shadow-traffic.explain:
## What it is

**Score production inputs without changing the user reply.** Shadow (or dark) traffic copies the request to a candidate prompt/model and scores both. The user still sees the control. You learn whether the candidate is safer before you flip.

This is A/B without the user risk.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviews: how to test a new prompt on real mix without shipping it. Shadow is the answer. On the job it also protects you from a candidate that is great offline and rude online.

## How it works + one small example

At request time, enqueue a copy. A worker runs the candidate. Store both outputs and scores. Never send the candidate to the user until a promotion rule fires.

Cap shadow QPS so you do not double-bill yourself into ruin.

## Failure modes

1. **Shadow that accidentally replies.**

2. **No QPS cap.**

3. **Comparing on different traces so it is not a pair.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Shadow scores real inputs on a candidate without changing the user reply. I pair the outputs, I cap QPS, and I promote only after the comparison.

## A concrete walk-through

A new groundedness prompt looks good offline. Shadow on 5% shows +0.04 faithfulness and +200ms. You promote for the P0 slice only.

## Interview follow-up

They ask vs A/B. A/B changes some users’ replies. Shadow does not.

## What I would measure

Shadow leak to users (0), paired coverage, $ of shadow traffic.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Shadow leak to users (0), paired coverage, $ of shadow traffic. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Shadow copies the request; the user still sees control. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: Shadow scores real inputs on a candidate without changing the user reply. I pair the outputs, I cap QPS, and I promote only after the comparison. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask vs A/B. A/B changes some users’ replies. Shadow does not. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Pair outputs for comparison.

## What would change my mind

Interviews: how to test a new prompt on real mix without shipping it. Shadow is the answer. On the job it also protects you from a candidate that is great offline and rude online. I change the design when a held-out slice moves, not when a demo is prettier. A third point that would force a redesign is: Cap QPS and $. One counter-example that lives in the golden set beats a week of vibe testing.

## How this shows up in a log

In a real trace I want to see the decision, the evidence, and the stop. A reviewer should be able to replay this walk-through from the log: A new groundedness prompt looks good offline. Shadow on 5% shows +0.04 faithfulness and +200ms. You promote for the P0 slice only. If the log cannot support that story, the feature is not observable yet. I also want the cheap how-it-works sketch nearby so a new teammate can implement the same check: At request time, enqueue a copy. A worker runs the candidate. Store both outputs and scores. Never send the candidate to the user until a promotion rule fires. Cap shadow QPS so you do not double-bill yourself into ruin.

A/B is the next step if you need user-visible effects.

questions.q: What is online shadow traffic?
questions.a: Scoring production inputs on a candidate system without changing the user-visible reply.

questions.q: How does it differ from A/B?
questions.a: A/B shows some users the candidate. Shadow never does.

questions.q: The candidate reply was sent to a user. What failed?
questions.a: The shadow path was wired to the response. Split the pipes.

questions.q: Why cap shadow QPS?
questions.a: You roughly double model spend. A cap keeps the experiment solvent.

questions.a: Paired control/candidate outputs, scores, and ids — redacted.

feedback-that-becomes-a-case.explain:
## What it is

**A thumbs-down with the retrieved context is tomorrow’s offline item.** Feedback without context is a mood. Feedback with the prompt, the chunks, the output and the user id (redacted) is a draft case.

Close the loop in one business day if you can.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the product phrasing of feeding failures back. Interviews want the fields you store on a thumbs-down.

## How it works + one small example

On downvote: snapshot `{input, context_ids, output, tools, user_hash, ts}`. Queue for triage. Label. PR. Do not store raw PII.

A thumbs-up can still yield a case if it is a rare good example of a hard slice.

## Failure modes

1. **Thumbs with no snapshot.**

2. **Snapshots with raw cards.**

3. **A queue nobody triages.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I snapshot input, context, output and tools on a thumbs-down. That snapshot is a draft gold case after redact and label.

## A concrete walk-through

You add the snapshot. Triage takes 10 minutes a day. Twelve cases a week enter gold. Recurrence of the same downvote reason falls.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about implicit feedback (edits, re-asks). Those are snapshots too.

## What I would measure

Snapshot completeness, triage lag, cases landed per week.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Snapshot completeness, triage lag, cases landed per week. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Downvote + context = draft case. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: I snapshot input, context, output and tools on a thumbs-down. That snapshot is a draft gold case after redact and label. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about implicit feedback (edits, re-asks). Those are snapshots too. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Snapshot input, chunks, output, tools.

## What would change my mind

This is the product phrasing of feeding failures back. Interviews want the fields you store on a thumbs-down. I change the design when a held-out slice moves, not when a demo is prettier. Twelve cases a week enter gold. Recurrence of the same downvote reason falls. If the log cannot support that story, the feature is not observable yet. core-llm-capabilities.explain:
## What it is

Model evaluations group abilities into a handful of **core capabilities**:

- **Knowledge and reasoning**: factual recall, multi-step logic, maths, commonsense.
- **Language**: comprehension, summarisation, translation, writing.
- **Coding**: generating, fixing and explaining code, often judged by running tests.
- **Instruction following**: obeying constraints on format, length and style.
- **Tool use and agency**: choosing and calling functions, multi-step tasks.
- **Long context**: finding and using information across large inputs.
- **Safety and honesty**: refusing harmful requests, avoiding fabrication.
- **Multimodal**: understanding images, audio or documents.

Why it matters: no model is best at everything, and capabilities trade against cost and latency. Map your product to the two or three capabilities that matter (e.g. extraction needs instruction following and long context) and weigh those benchmarks, not the headline average.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

When you read a bench, name the capability: knowledge, reasoning, maths, coding, instruction following, long context, multimodal, safety, tool use. A win on maths is not a win on your JSON-extract job.

Interviews: map your product to two capabilities.

## How it works + one small example

Write the product’s needed capabilities first. Then look at benches that claim those. Long-doc extract → long context + instruction following + structured output. Not GPQA.

A model card that only shows the shiny capability is a marketing card.

## Failure modes

1. **Buying a maths champ for a classifier.**

2. **Ignoring tool-use benches for an agent.**

3. **Treating “general intelligence” as a capability you can measure once.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I map the product to capabilities, then I read the benches that claim those. A maths trophy is not an extract trophy.

## A concrete walk-through

You need long-context extract. You shortlist models with long-context and schema-following numbers, not the ones topping a maths contest.

## Interview follow-up

They list ten benches. You pick two and say why the rest are noise for this job.

## What I would measure

Whether your shortlist memo names capabilities.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Whether your shortlist memo names capabilities. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Name capabilities before benches. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: I map the product to capabilities, then I read the benches that claim those. A maths trophy is not an extract trophy. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They list ten benches. You pick two and say why the rest are noise for this job. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Map product → capabilities → benches.
keyPoints: A card that only shows the shiny skill is marketing.
Tool use is a capability of its own.
Safety is a capability, not a vibe.
Capabilities: knowledge, reasoning, language, coding, instruction following, tools, long context, safety
No model is best at all; weight what your product needs

questions.q: List core LLM capabilities evaluated by benchmarks.
questions.a: Knowledge and reasoning, language tasks, coding, instruction following, tool use or agency, long-context use, safety and honesty, and multimodal understanding. Each has its own benchmarks and none is sufficient alone.

questions.q: You build a contract-clause extractor. Which capabilities should drive model choice?
questions.a: Instruction following and structured output reliability, long-context retrieval accuracy, and low hallucination. Prioritise those evaluations over maths or coding scores, then confirm on your own contract samples.

questions.q: You choose a model for long-document extraction. Which capability focus?
questions.a: Long-context retrieval and structured-output instruction following — not competition maths.

questions.q: List several core LLM capabilities benches try to measure.
questions.a: Knowledge, reasoning, maths, coding, instruction following, long context, multimodal, safety, tool use.

questions.q: Why is “best overall model” a weak phrase?
questions.a: Overall averages hide the capability you need and the one you do not.

questions.q: An agent product ignores tool-use benches. Risk?
questions.a: You may pick a fluent model that cannot call functions reliably.

anatomy-of-a-benchmark.explain:
## What it is

A **benchmark** has parts you should be able to name:

- **Task definition**: what the model is asked to do.
- **Dataset**: the items, often with a held-out test split.
- **Prompt format**: zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought, system prompt, answer format.
- **Scoring rule**: exact match, multiple-choice accuracy, pass@k for code, or a judge.
- **Aggregation**: per-task and overall averages, sometimes weighted.
- **Harness and settings**: sampling temperature, number of shots, answer extraction, version.

Small details change scores a lot: the same model can differ by several points with a different prompt template or answer parser. So a reported number is only comparable when the harness and settings match. Good benchmarks are valid (measure what they claim), reliable (low noise), discriminative (separate models) and hard to contaminate.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

A benchmark is a dataset, prompts, run config, scoring method and aggregation. Change any piece and the number moves. Two papers with the same name can be incomparable.

Interviews: list the five parts.

## How it works + one small example

When you read a score, ask: which split, how many shots, what parse, what temperature, which version of the set. If the report omits them, treat the number as decoration.

When you run one, record all five in the artefact.

## Failure modes

1. **Comparing scores from different harnesses as if equal.**

2. **A custom prompt that inflates your favourite model.**

3. **Aggregation that hides a dead slice.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

A bench is dataset + prompt + config + scorer + aggregation. I do not compare numbers that do not share those parts.

## A concrete walk-through

Two “MMLU” numbers differ by 4 points. One is 5-shot, one 0-shot. You stop arguing and rerun both in one harness.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about leaderboards. Same anatomy; plus they may hide the harness.

## What I would measure

Reports you rejected for missing anatomy, harness-controlled reruns.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Reports you rejected for missing anatomy, harness-controlled reruns. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Five parts: data, prompts, config, score, aggregation. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: A bench is dataset + prompt + config + scorer + aggregation. I do not compare numbers that do not share those parts. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about leaderboards. Same anatomy; plus they may hide the harness. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Harness differences move scores.
keyPoints: Five parts: data, prompts, config, score, aggregation.
Record all five when you run.
A name is not a protocol.
Task, dataset, prompt format, scoring, aggregation and harness
Prompt and parser details can shift scores a lot

questions.q: What components make up a benchmark?
questions.a: Task definition, dataset with a test split, prompt format (shots, CoT), scoring rule, aggregation method, and the harness settings such as temperature and answer extraction. Scores are only comparable when these match.

questions.q: Two vendors report different MMLU-style scores for the same model. Why?
questions.a: Different prompt templates, number of shots, CoT usage, answer extraction or dataset versions. Rerun both under one harness with identical settings before comparing.

questions.q: Two reports disagree on the same named benchmark. Most probable explanation?
questions.a: Different prompts, shots, parsing or dataset versions.

questions.q: What is the anatomy of a benchmark?
questions.a: Dataset, prompts, run configuration, scoring method, and aggregation.

questions.q: What do you store when you run one?
questions.a: All five parts plus the model id and date.

questions.q: A leaderboard hides the prompt. Problem?
questions.a: You cannot reproduce or compare. Treat the rank as a hint.

public-leaderboards.explain:
## What it is

**Public leaderboards** rank models by benchmark scores or by crowd preference (e.g. pairwise human votes aggregated into ratings). They give a quick, free view of the frontier and help build a shortlist.

How to read them:
- Check what the leaderboard measures: static benchmark accuracy, human preference, or task-specific scores.
- Look at confidence intervals; adjacent ranks are often statistically tied.
- Note the settings, date and model version.
- Beware that preference rankings can reward style and length.

What they cannot tell you: performance on your data, your prompts, your latency and cost limits, or safety in your context. Treat a leaderboard as a map of candidates, never as the decision. In interviews, state that you use it for shortlisting and then run a custom eval.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Leaderboards compare foundation models under one harness — in theory. In practice: contamination, self-reports, closed evals, and confidence intervals that overlap. Use them to shortlist, not to crown.

Read the error bars.

## How it works + one small example

Pick a board that publishes the harness and CIs. Shortlist models whose intervals do not collapse into each other on the capability you need. Then run your set.

If rank 2 and 3 overlap, they are a tie for your purposes.

## Failure modes

1. **Picking rank 1 as a final decision.**

2. **Ignoring CIs.**

3. **A board that does not publish the harness.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Leaderboards shortlist. Overlapping CIs are a tie. I still run my application eval.

## A concrete walk-through

Rank 1 and 2 overlap on the board you care about. You test both. The cheaper one wins your set. You ship that.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about Elo chat boards. Preference ≠ task success. Say so.

## What I would measure

How often you treated overlap as a tie, rank-only decisions (0).

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: How often you treated overlap as a tie, rank-only decisions (0). That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Boards are a shortlist tool. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: Leaderboards shortlist. Overlapping CIs are a tie. I still run my application eval. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about Elo chat boards. Preference ≠ task success. Say so. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Read CIs; overlap = tie.

## What would change my mind

Leaderboards compare foundation models under one harness — in theory. In practice: contamination, self-reports, closed evals, and confidence intervals that overlap. Use them to shortlist, not to crown. Read the error bars. I change the design when a held-out slice moves, not when a demo is prettier. A third point that would force a redesign is: Need a published harness. One counter-example that lives in the golden set beats a week of vibe testing.
keyPoints: Preference Elo is not task success.
Check measure, confidence intervals, versions and dates

questions.q: How should an engineer use public leaderboards?
questions.a: To shortlist candidates and track the frontier, reading what is measured, confidence intervals and versions. The final choice should come from a custom eval on your task with cost and latency included.

questions.q: Model A ranks one place above B on a preference leaderboard. Should you pick A?
questions.a: Not on that alone: the gap may be within confidence intervals, preference voting can favour verbose or stylish answers, and your task differs. Test both on your own dataset including cost and latency.

questions.q: Rank 2 and 3 have overlapping CIs. What does that tell you?
questions.a: They are statistically indistinguishable on that measure.

questions.q: Best use of leaderboard results?
questions.a: Shortlisting before a custom eval on your data.

questions.q: A chat Elo board is won by a witty model. Relevance to extract?
questions.a: Low. Preference is not structured-output skill.

questions.q: What must a trustworthy board publish?
questions.a: Harness details, dataset version, and uncertainty.

benchmark-pitfalls.explain:
## What it is

Common ways benchmark numbers mislead:

- **Contamination**: test items leaked into training data, so the model memorised answers.
- **Saturation**: top models score near the ceiling, so differences are noise.
- **Overfitting to the benchmark** (Goodhart's law): labs optimise for the metric.
- **Label errors** and ambiguous questions cap the true ceiling.
- **Prompt sensitivity**: small format changes move scores.
- **Narrow validity**: multiple choice does not predict open-ended generation.
- **Selective reporting**: vendors show benchmarks they win.
- **Noise**: small test sets give wide intervals.

Defences: use fresh or private held-out sets, report variance, evaluate on your own task, combine several benchmarks, and read the methodology. A strong answer names contamination and saturation first.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Pitfalls: contamination (train on the test), saturation (everyone scores 90), overfitting to the bench, configuration gaming (the perfect prompt). Interviews: name four and how you notice.

## How it works + one small example

Notice contamination: paraphrase the items and watch the drop. Saturation: look at the ceiling and the label noise. Overfit: a model that only shines on one set. Gaming: unusual prompts or voting schemes.

Your defence is a private set.

## Failure modes

1. **Treating a saturated bench as a ranking tool.**

2. **Tuning prompts for weeks on a public set you will report.**

3. **Ignoring paraphrase drops.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I watch for contamination, saturation, overfit and gaming. A private set is the defence. A 90% public number may mean the bench died.

## A concrete walk-through

A model is 92% on a public set and 61% on your paraphrases. You treat the public number as contaminated and decide on your set.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about decontamination methods. Mention n-gram overlap checks, but still prefer private data.

## What I would measure

Paraphrase drops, benches you retired for saturation.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Paraphrase drops, benches you retired for saturation. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Contamination, saturation, overfit, gaming. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: I watch for contamination, saturation, overfit and gaming. A private set is the defence. A 90% public number may mean the bench died. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about decontamination methods. Mention n-gram overlap checks, but still prefer private data. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Paraphrase to probe memorisation.
keyPoints: Do not tune on the set you will brag about.
Label noise plus ceiling = junk deltas.
Contamination and saturation are the headline problems
Prompt sensitivity, label errors and Goodhart effects distort scores

questions.q: What is benchmark contamination and why does it matter?
questions.a: Test data appearing in the training corpus so the model has seen the answers, inflating scores without real ability. Counter with private or newly created test sets, canary strings and analysis of memorisation.

questions.q: A benchmark shows 97% for several top models. How do you interpret that?
questions.a: It is likely saturated, so remaining differences are within noise or label error and no longer discriminate. Move to harder or task-specific evals.

questions.q: A model aces a public bench but fails paraphrases. Likely cause?
questions.a: Contamination or memorisation of the original items.

questions.q: Name four benchmark pitfalls.
questions.a: Data contamination, score saturation, overfitting to the bench, and configuration gaming.

questions.q: When does a bench stop discriminating?
questions.a: When most frontier models sit at the ceiling and deltas are label noise.

questions.q: What is configuration gaming?
questions.a: A special prompt, parse or vote that inflates one model on that harness.

task-transfer-is-the-real-test.explain:
## What it is

**A leaderboard win that fails your tickets is not a win.** Transfer is whether capability on a public task shows up on your distribution. It often does not. The real test is your tickets, your JSON, your language mix.

This is the application-eval principle said as a bench warning.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interview closer for M7.4. They quote a rank. You quote your set.

## How it works + one small example

Whenever someone pastes a rank, run the top two on 50 of your tickets the same day. Write both numbers in the thread. Culture changes.

## Failure modes

1. **Delaying your set “until we pick a model.”**

2. **Declaring transfer without a number.**

3. **Tickets that are themselves leaked public items.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Transfer is the test. A leaderboard win that fails our tickets is not a win. I run the tickets the same day.

## A concrete walk-through

Rank 1 fails your Hindi refund tickets. Rank 3 passes. You pick 3. The Slack thread has the table.

## Interview follow-up

They ask how many tickets. Fifty diverse beats five demos.

## What I would measure

Same-day transfer runs, rank-only picks (0).

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Same-day transfer runs, rank-only picks (0). That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Your tickets are the transfer test. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: Transfer is the test. A leaderboard win that fails our tickets is not a win. I run the tickets the same day. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask how many tickets. Fifty diverse beats five demos. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: A public win can fail privately.

## What would change my mind

Interview closer for M7.4. They quote a rank. You quote your set. I change the design when a held-out slice moves, not when a demo is prettier. A third point that would force a redesign is: Run the comparison the same day. One counter-example that lives in the golden set beats a week of vibe testing.

## How this shows up in a log

In a real trace I want to see the decision, the evidence, and the stop. A reviewer should be able to replay this walk-through from the log: Rank 1 fails your Hindi refund tickets. Rank 3 passes. You pick 3. The Slack thread has the table. If the log cannot support that story, the feature is not observable yet. I also want the cheap how-it-works sketch nearby so a new teammate can implement the same check: Whenever someone pastes a rank, run the top two on 50 of your tickets the same day. Write both numbers in the thread. Culture changes.
keyPoints: Your tickets are the transfer test.
A public win can fail privately.
Run the comparison the same day.
Fifty diverse tickets beat five demos.
Do not delay your set until after the pick.
Watch for leaked public items in “your” tickets.

questions.q: What is the real test of a leaderboard win?
questions.a: Whether it transfers to your tickets and formats — measured, not assumed.

questions.q: Rank 1 fails your tickets; rank 3 passes. What do you ship?
questions.a: Rank 3, and you keep the table.

questions.q: Why same day?
questions.a: So the rank does not become a decision while you “plan” an eval.

questions.q: Your tickets are copies of MMLU. Problem?
questions.a: That is not transfer. It is the same bench in disguise.

questions.q: How many tickets to start?
questions.a: About fifty diverse ones, including recent misses.

reading-a-model-card-like-a-sceptic.explain:
## What it is

**Training data, cutoff, safety, and the eval they chose to show.** A sceptical reading of a model card asks those four, plus licence, context length, and what they omitted. The eval they chose is the ad. The cutoff tells you if your 2026 policy is invisible.

Cards are marketing with a PDF badge.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interview skill: they paste a card. You ask what is missing. On the job this is procurement.

## How it works + one small example

Checklist: cutoff date, data claims (and what they cannot say), safety evals (and the ones not shown), context, pricing, licence, region, tool-use claims. Compare to a second card on the same axes.

If safety is a paragraph with no number, treat it as unmeasured.

## Failure modes

1. **Reading only the lead sentence.**

2. **Ignoring licence until launch.**

3. **Believing “trained on the internet” as a coverage guarantee.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I read a card for cutoff, data, safety numbers, the eval they chose to show, licence and context. What they omitted is data too.

## A concrete walk-through

A card boasts MMLU and hides a weak tool-use number in a footnote. You need tools. You put that footnote in the shortlist memo.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about “constitutional” adjectives. You want numbers.

## What I would measure

Memos that cite omissions, licences caught before build.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Memos that cite omissions, licences caught before build. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Read cutoff, data, safety, shown evals, licence, context. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: I read a card for cutoff, data, safety numbers, the eval they chose to show, licence and context. What they omitted is data too. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about “constitutional” adjectives. You want numbers. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: The shown eval is an ad.

## What would change my mind

Interview skill: they paste a card. You ask what is missing. On the job this is procurement. I change the design when a held-out slice moves, not when a demo is prettier. A third point that would force a redesign is: Omission is information. One counter-example that lives in the golden set beats a week of vibe testing.

## How this shows up in a log

In a real trace I want to see the decision, the evidence, and the stop. A reviewer should be able to replay this walk-through from the log: A card boasts MMLU and hides a weak tool-use number in a footnote. You need tools. You put that footnote in the shortlist memo. from-mmlu-to-harder-knowledge-tests.explain:
## What it is

**MMLU** (Massive Multitask Language Understanding) tests multiple-choice knowledge across dozens of subjects, from law to chemistry. When it appeared, models scored far below humans; as models improved, frontier scores climbed close to the ceiling, so MMLU stopped separating the best models.

Several problems emerged: some questions have wrong or ambiguous labels, contamination risk grew as the dataset spread across the web, and four-option multiple choice lets guessing and elimination pad scores.

The response was a ladder of harder successors: more options, harder reasoning-heavy questions, expert-written problems that search cannot answer, and tests of factual honesty. The pattern is general: a benchmark's useful life ends when strong models saturate it, so the field keeps replacing it.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

MMLU and TruthfulQA were the knowledge/honesty pair. Frontier models saturated MMLU and exposed label noise. The field moved to harder, cleaner, or more contamination-resistant tests. Interviews: why the move, not a trivia list.

## How it works + one small example

MMLU: broad multiple choice, now a ceiling. TruthfulQA: imitative falsehoods, still useful for honesty. Harder follow-ons raise expert difficulty or reduce shortcut answers.

Use them as history. Your product set is still the decision.

## Failure modes

1. **Still ranking production models on raw MMLU.**

2. **Treating TruthfulQA as a safety full suite.**

3. **Memorising years instead of the reason.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

We left MMLU as a ranking tool because it saturated and its labels are noisy. Harder knowledge tests exist; my product set still decides.

## A concrete walk-through

A vendor waves MMLU 90%. You ask for a harder set and your tickets. The conversation gets useful.

## Interview follow-up

They ask TruthfulQA vs SimpleQA. Honesty/imitative falsehoods vs short fact accuracy — different jobs.

## What I would measure

Whether your memos still lead with MMLU (they should not).

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Whether your memos still lead with MMLU (they should not). That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: MMLU saturated and is noisy. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: We left MMLU as a ranking tool because it saturated and its labels are noisy. Harder knowledge tests exist; my product set still decides. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask TruthfulQA vs SimpleQA. Honesty/imitative falsehoods vs short fact accuracy — different jobs. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: TruthfulQA is honesty, not all of safety.

Do not rank prod models on a dead bench.

questions.a: Top models approached its ceiling so differences became noise, labels contain errors, contamination is plausible and four-option guessing inflates scores. Harder benchmarks were created to restore discrimination.

questions.q: What does the MMLU history teach about relying on a single benchmark?
questions.a: Benchmarks have a lifecycle: they discriminate until models saturate or leak into training data. You should combine current benchmarks and your own evals and expect to retire old ones.

questions.q: What is the main weakness of MMLU for today’s best models?
questions.a: Scores near the ceiling and label errors, so differences are noise.

questions.q: Why did knowledge benches get harder?
questions.a: Frontier models saturated older sets, so they stopped discriminating.

questions.a: No. It targets imitative falsehoods, not the whole harm surface.

questions.a: Ask for a harder set and your own transfer run.

human-exams-as-benchmarks.explain:
## What it is

Labs often report scores on **human exams**: bar exam, medical licensing, AP tests, olympiads, coding contests. They are attractive because they are authored by experts, have recognised difficulty and give an intuitive comparison to people.

Caveats:
- **Contamination**: past papers and solutions are online.
- **Format mismatch**: exams test humans under time limits, with grading designed around human errors; passing does not mean professional competence.
- **Narrow slice**: multiple choice and essays do not cover real work such as dealing with clients.
- **Reporting choices**: shots, tools, retries and partial credit differ between reports.

Use exam results as a rough indication of reasoning at a level, not as proof the model can do the job. Prefer recently released exams for contamination resistance.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Exams (bar, medical, AGIEval-style) are tempting because humans have scores. They are also public, coachable, and a thin proxy for the job. Contamination is common. Interviewers want that caution.

## How it works + one small example

If you cite an exam number, add: public items may be in the train, exam skill ≠ job skill, format artefacts (MCQ). Prefer private professional tasks.

AGIEval-style suites try to be cleaner; still not your tickets.

## Failure modes

1. **“It passed the bar” as a hire-the-model argument.**

2. **Ignoring that past papers are on GitHub.**

3. **MCQ exam skill as proof of open-ended advice quality.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Human exams are contaminated, coachable proxies. I may use them as a filter, not as proof the model can do the job.

## A concrete walk-through

A model “passes” a public bar set and fails your firm’s memo task. You write that in the shortlist. Legal stops quoting the bar number.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about live exams. Better, still a proxy, still not your workflow.

## What I would measure

Exam numbers used as final decisions (0).

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Exam numbers used as final decisions (0). That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Exams are public and coachable. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: Human exams are contaminated, coachable proxies. I may use them as a filter, not as proof the model can do the job. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about live exams. Better, still a proxy, still not your workflow. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Exam skill ≠ job skill.
keyPoints: Use as a filter, not a proof.
Contamination and format mismatch limit meaning

questions.q: Why are human exams used as LLM benchmarks and what is the catch?
questions.a: They are expert-authored, have known difficulty and compare to people. Catches: question leakage into training data, format and reporting differences, and the gap between exam performance and real professional work.

questions.q: A model passes a medical licensing exam. Can you deploy it for patient advice?
questions.a: No. The exam is a narrow proxy that may be contaminated; deployment needs task-specific evaluation, safety testing, clinician review and risk controls.

questions.a: Contamination and proxy validity: exam skill is not job competence.

questions.q: Why use exams at all?
questions.a: As a coarse filter of professional-style questions, not as the decision.

questions.q: What format artefact shows up?
questions.a: Multiple-choice test-taking tricks that do not transfer to open memos.

questions.q: Live proctored exams vs GitHub past papers?
questions.a: Live is less contaminated; still a proxy for your workflow.

gpqa-mmlu-pro-simpleqa-hle.explain:
## What it is

Four well-known successors, each targeting a gap:

- **MMLU-Pro**: harder MMLU variant with more answer options and more reasoning-heavy questions, reducing guessing and some noise.
- **GPQA**: graduate-level science questions written and validated by domain experts, designed to be "Google-proof" so search does not trivially help; the hard subset is used to measure expert-level reasoning.
- **SimpleQA**: short factual questions with one verifiable answer, used to measure factual accuracy and whether the model abstains rather than hallucinates.
- **Humanity's Last Exam (HLE)**: a very hard, broad set of expert-submitted questions intended to stay unsaturated for longer.

For interviews know the purpose of each, not the scores (they change fast): reasoning difficulty, expert grading, factuality/abstention, and frontier-difficulty. Check current leaderboards for numbers.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Harder sets you should be able to place: GPQA (expert, “Google-proof”), MMLU-Pro (harder MMLU), SimpleQA (short facts, calibration), Humanity’s Last Exam (very hard expert). Know what each claims, not every score.

## How it works + one small example

GPQA: graduate-level, hard to search. MMLU-Pro: more options, harder items. SimpleQA: short verifiable answers, tracks attempted vs correct. HLE: a small, brutal expert set.

Use SimpleQA-like thinking for hallucination rate. Use GPQA as a filter for “reasoners.” Neither replaces tickets.

## Failure modes

1. **Treating HLE as a product KPI.**

2. **Confusing SimpleQA with MMLU.**

3. **Quoting a number without the set’s job.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

GPQA and MMLU-Pro raise knowledge difficulty; SimpleQA measures short-fact honesty; HLE is a tiny expert ceiling. I place them; I do not KPI them.

## A concrete walk-through

You care about fabricated facts. You look at SimpleQA-style attempted-vs-correct, then you build a 40-fact set from your domain.

## Interview follow-up

They ask “Google-proof.” It means hard to answer by naive search, not “unsearchable forever.”

## What I would measure

Whether you can define each in one clause.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Whether you can define each in one clause. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: GPQA: expert, hard to naive-search. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: GPQA and MMLU-Pro raise knowledge difficulty; SimpleQA measures short-fact honesty; HLE is a tiny expert ceiling. I place them; I do not KPI them. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask “Google-proof.” It means hard to answer by naive search, not “unsearchable forever.” I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: MMLU-Pro: harder MMLU.

MMLU-Pro: more options and reasoning; GPQA: expert Google-proof science
SimpleQA: short factual accuracy and hallucination rate

questions.q: What gap does SimpleQA address that GPQA does not?
questions.a: SimpleQA measures short-form factual accuracy and hallucination or abstention behaviour with single verifiable answers, whereas GPQA tests expert-level scientific reasoning in multiple choice.

questions.q: Which benchmark would you check for hallucination tendency on factual lookups and why?
questions.a: SimpleQA-style evaluation, since questions have one verifiable answer and scoring separates correct, incorrect and not-attempted, revealing overconfident fabrication.

questions.q: Why is GPQA described as Google-proof?
questions.a: Expert-written questions that are hard to answer by simple web search.

questions.q: Which bench best measures fabricated short facts?
questions.a: SimpleQA (or a domain clone): short verifiable answers, incorrect vs not-attempted.

questions.q: Should HLE be your product KPI?
questions.a: No. It is a tiny expert ceiling. Use your tickets.

questions.q: What did MMLU-Pro change versus MMLU?
questions.a: Harder items and a format that reduces easy guessing.

why-benchmarks-keep-getting-harder.explain:
## What it is

Benchmarks get harder because **models improve faster than tests are written**. A benchmark that separates models today saturates in a year or two.

Drivers:
- **Saturation**: scores near the ceiling stop discriminating.
- **Contamination**: public benchmarks leak into training data, forcing new private or fresh sets.
- **Optimisation pressure**: labs tune to popular benchmarks (Goodhart's law).
- **Capability growth**: reasoning models solve what once looked impossible, so test designers recruit experts for harder questions.
- **Cost of creation**: expert-written questions are expensive, so each new set is smaller and noisier.

Implication for engineers: treat public benchmark scores as short-lived. Your product eval should stay relevant because it is tied to your tasks, and you should keep it updated rather than expecting a permanent standard.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Benches harden because models catch up, items leak, and a ceiling stops ranking. The economics: expert items are expensive, so new sets are smaller and noisier. Interviews: this loop, plus “so I need my own set.”

## How it works + one small example

Story: publish set → models train/leak/saturate → rank dies → new harder set → repeat. Your escape is private, refreshed data.

Small expert sets have wide CIs — do not over-read a 2-point delta.

## Failure modes

1. **Chasing the newest bench as a personality.**

2. **Over-reading tiny hard sets.**

3. **Not refreshing your private set.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Benches harden because old ones saturate and leak. New ones are smaller and noisier. I escape the loop with a private, living set.

## A concrete walk-through

You stopped quoting the newest three-letter exam each month. You invested in 80 living tickets. The ranking arguments died; the product improved.

## Interview follow-up

They ask if the loop ever ends. Not while models improve and items leak.

## What I would measure

How often your memos cite a new public bench vs your set.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: How often your memos cite a new public bench vs your set. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Saturate → leak → harden → repeat. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: Benches harden because old ones saturate and leak. New ones are smaller and noisier. I escape the loop with a private, living set. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask if the loop ever ends. Not while models improve and items leak. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Expert items are costly, so new sets are small.

questions.a: Only as a time-limited indicator. Check the date, the saturation level and contamination risk, and anchor decisions on a maintained, task-specific eval.

questions.a: A private, refreshed product set.

questions.a: Wide CI. Do not ship on that delta alone.

saturation-means-you-need-a-harder-set.explain:
## What it is

**When everyone scores 90, the benchmark stopped discriminating.** Saturation is a property of the set plus the current models, not a property of intelligence. You need harder or different items — or you need a different metric (calibration, cost, tail fails).

A saturated set can still catch a broken build if a model collapses. It cannot pick a winner.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

The checklist closer for M7.5. Interviews: define saturation and say what you do next.

## How it works + one small example

Look at the score histogram. If the frontier cluster is at the ceiling, retire the set for ranking. Keep it as a smoke “did we break everything?” Or add harder items / a new slice.

Do not average in a saturated set to make a marketing overall.

## Failure modes

1. **Picking a winner on 91 vs 92 on a noisy saturated set.**

2. **Deleting the set entirely so you miss a collapse.**

3. **Hiding saturation in an average.**

When everyone scores 90, I stop ranking on that set. I keep it as smoke or I replace it. I do not advertise 92 vs 91.

Your public clone of MMLU is 89–93 for all candidates. You retire it for ranking, keep 30 items as smoke, and decide on 80 product tickets.

## Interview follow-up

Sets retired for ranking, smoke sets kept.

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Sets retired for ranking, smoke sets kept. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. human-exams-vs-product-tasks.explain:
## What it is

**GPQA is a filter, not a substitute for your tickets.** Human-exam and expert-knowledge sets tell you something about hard QA. They do not tell you if the model can file your refund, emit your schema, or stay in your tone.

Use them to drop hopeless models. Decide on product tasks.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

The last M7.5 line. Interviews: filter vs decide. On the job, stop a thread that quotes GPQA as the v1 metric.

## How it works + one small example

Stage 1: drop models that fail a hard QA or instruction filter you care about. Stage 2: 80 product tasks. Never skip stage 2 because stage 1 looked glorious.

If your product is not expert QA, GPQA can be a weak filter — skip it.

## Failure modes

1. **GPQA as the KPI.**

2. **Skipping product tasks because the filter was impressive.**

3. **Using GPQA for a classifier product.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Expert exams filter. Product tasks decide. GPQA is not a substitute for our tickets.

## A concrete walk-through

A model is great on GPQA and cannot keep a 4-field JSON schema. You drop it at stage 2 and the GPQA number never appears in the launch mail.

## Interview follow-up

They ask which filter for a SQL agent. Text-to-SQL benches or your own schemas — not HLE.

## What I would measure

Launches whose KPI was a public exam (0).

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Launches whose KPI was a public exam (0). That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Expert sets filter; tickets decide. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

GPQA is not a substitute for our tickets. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask which filter for a SQL agent. Text-to-SQL benches or your own schemas — not HLE. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Skip the filter if it is the wrong skill.

## What would change my mind

The last M7.5 line. Interviews: filter vs decide. On the job, stop a thread that quotes GPQA as the v1 metric. I change the design when a held-out slice moves, not when a demo is prettier. A third point that would force a redesign is: Never skip product tasks. One counter-example that lives in the golden set beats a week of vibe testing.

## How this shows up in a log

In a real trace I want to see the decision, the evidence, and the stop. A reviewer should be able to replay this walk-through from the log: A model is great on GPQA and cannot keep a 4-field JSON schema. You drop it at stage 2 and the GPQA number never appears in the launch mail. If the log cannot support that story, the feature is not observable yet. I also want the cheap how-it-works sketch nearby so a new teammate can implement the same check: Stage 1: drop models that fail a hard QA or instruction filter you care about. Stage 2: 80 product tasks. Never skip stage 2 because stage 1 looked glorious. If your product is not expert QA, GPQA can be a weak filter — skip it.

questions.a: When the product does not need expert QA (e.g. a classifier or a formatter).
