questions.q: Can a product-task set be small at first?
questions.a: Yes. Fifty good tickets beat a glorious filter with no tickets.

evaluating-on-your-actual-task.explain:
## What it is

Public benchmarks measure generic skills; **your task** has specific inputs, formats, domain vocabulary and failure costs. Evaluate on that.

How:
- Write down the task in one sentence and what a good output looks like.
- Collect real inputs (from logs, tickets, documents), not invented ones.
- Define pass criteria per case: a reference answer, a checklist, or a rubric.
- Run each candidate with your real prompt, retrieval and tools.
- Examine failures by reading them.

A model that is second on a leaderboard can be first on your task because of format handling, domain jargon or instruction style. Even 50 to 100 well-chosen cases usually reveals clear differences. Interview line: "benchmarks tell me where to look, my eval tells me what to ship".

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Public benches are someone else’s task. Your task has your formats, jargon, languages and failure modes. Custom eval is how a “weaker” model wins.

Interviews: start here, not with a board.

## How it works + one small example

Write 50–150 inputs that look like production. Define success. Run candidates the same way the app will (same tools, same RAG). That number is the decision.

Include the last ten production misses on purpose.

## Failure modes

1. **A “custom” set that is just MMLU clones.**

2. **Running without the retriever the app uses.**

3. **Only easy cases.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I evaluate on the actual task, with the actual pipeline, including recent misses. A public bench is a shortlist hint.

## A concrete walk-through

A mid-rank model wins your Text-to-SQL set because it follows your dialect. You ship it. The leaderboard crowd is confused; your p95 latency is not.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about size. Start 50, grow from misses.

## What I would measure

Share of cases that look like prod, pipeline-faithful runs.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Share of cases that look like prod, pipeline-faithful runs. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Your task, your pipeline, your misses. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: I evaluate on the actual task, with the actual pipeline, including recent misses. A public bench is a shortlist hint. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about size. Start 50, grow from misses. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Public benches shortlist.

## What would change my mind

Public benches are someone else’s task. Your task has your formats, jargon, languages and failure modes. Custom eval is how a “weaker” model wins. Interviews: start here, not with a board. I change the design when a held-out slice moves, not when a demo is prettier. A third point that would force a redesign is: Do not clone MMLU and call it custom. One counter-example that lives in the golden set beats a week of vibe testing.
keyPoints: Your task, your pipeline, your misses.
Do not clone MMLU and call it custom.
A weaker public model can win.
Use real inputs, your prompts and your success criteria
Small representative sets often show clear differences

questions.q: Why evaluate on your actual task instead of relying on benchmarks?
questions.a: Benchmarks test generic skills under their own prompts; your task has its own inputs, formats, domain language and costs of failure. Only a task eval shows which model works with your pipeline.

questions.q: How many cases do you need to start, and what matters more than count?
questions.a: A few dozen to a hundred is enough to start; what matters is representativeness, coverage of categories and edge cases, and clear criteria. Grow it from failures.

questions.q: Why can a lower-ranked model win your internal eval?
questions.a: It fits your formats, domain language and instructions better.

questions.q: What makes a set “actual task”?
questions.a: Real or realistic inputs, the production pipeline, and recent misses.

questions.q: You eval the model without the retriever the app uses. Problem?
questions.a: You measured a different system. Include retrieval.

questions.q: How do you start the set?
questions.a: Fifty diverse prod-like cases, then grow from misses.

shortlisting-candidate-models.explain:
## What it is

With hundreds of models, you cannot test all. **Shortlist** to three to five using cheap filters:

- **Hard constraints**: context window, modalities, structured output or tool support, data residency, licence, hosting (API vs self-hosted).
- **Budget limits**: price per token and rate limits, latency targets.
- **Capability fit**: relevant benchmarks and leaderboards for your core capabilities.
- **Diversity**: include a frontier model, a cheaper mid-tier one and maybe a small or open model, so you see the quality/cost curve.

Then run the custom eval on that list. Re-shortlist periodically as new models appear. A common mistake is only testing the most famous model and so never learning whether a cheaper one is good enough.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Shortlist with public signals: capability, context, latency, price, region, licence. Do not shortlist 15 models you will not run. Three to five is enough.

A shortlist memo is a page, not a spreadsheet of dreams.

## How it works + one small example

Must-haves: context size, region, licence, max $ / 1M tokens. Nice-to-haves: board scores on the right capability. Drop the rest. Then custom-eval the survivors.

Include at least one cheap model so you learn the quality/cost curve.

## Failure modes

1. **Shortlisting only frontier models.**

2. **Ignoring licence.**

3. **Fifteen candidates, no time to eval.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I shortlist 3–5 models on capability, context, latency, cost, region and licence — including a cheap one — then I custom-eval.

## A concrete walk-through

Must-have: 128k, EU region, < $X. Four models remain. You run the 80 cases. The cheapest acceptable wins.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about open weights. They are a candidate if licence and ops fit.

## What I would measure

Shortlist size, must-have violations that still entered the eval.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Shortlist size, must-have violations that still entered the eval. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: 3–5 candidates, not 15. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: I shortlist 3–5 models on capability, context, latency, cost, region and licence — including a cheap one — then I custom-eval. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about open weights. They are a candidate if licence and ops fit. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Must-haves: context, region, licence, price.

## What would change my mind

Shortlist with public signals: capability, context, latency, price, region, licence. Do not shortlist 15 models you will not run. Three to five is enough. A shortlist memo is a page, not a spreadsheet of dreams. I change the design when a held-out slice moves, not when a demo is prettier. A third point that would force a redesign is: Include a cheap model. One counter-example that lives in the golden set beats a week of vibe testing.
keyPoints: Boards inform, they do not pick.
Open weights are a path, not a free pass.
Filter by hard constraints, budget and capability fit
Include different tiers to see the cost curve

questions.q: What criteria do you use to shortlist models?
questions.a: Hard constraints (context, modalities, tool/JSON support, residency, licence), budget and latency limits, capability fit from relevant benchmarks, plus tier diversity so the quality/cost trade-off is visible.

questions.q: Why include a small cheap model in your shortlist even if you expect it to lose?
questions.a: It may be good enough for some or all categories, which can cut cost greatly or support routing easy queries to it. Testing shows how much quality you would trade.

questions.q: What do you use leaderboards for in selection?
questions.a: To shortlist on capability, then custom-eval — not to decide.

questions.q: Why include a cheap model in the shortlist?
questions.a: To learn the quality/cost curve and to have a fallback.

questions.q: A model fails the region must-have. Eval it?
questions.a: No. Must-haves are filters.

questions.q: How many candidates can you honestly eval?
questions.a: About three to five on a real set.

building-a-custom-eval-dataset.explain:
## What it is

Steps to build a dataset for model comparison:

1. **Source inputs** from production logs, support tickets, documents and subject-matter experts. Synthetic generation can fill gaps but must be reviewed.
2. **Stratify** by category, difficulty and user type so rare but important cases appear.
3. **Label**: write reference answers or rubrics; have two reviewers on a subset and measure agreement.
4. **Include hard negatives**: ambiguous queries, out-of-scope questions, adversarial input.
5. **Split**: keep a held-out test set that you never tune prompts against.
6. **Document and version**: provenance, labelling guide, date.

Anonymise personal data. Pitfalls: only easy cases, labels written by the model under test, and leakage of test cases into few-shot examples.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

A custom set for a real task (Text-to-SQL is the usual example) needs inputs, schemas, expected queries or results, and tags. Independent labels. A labelling guide.

The set is the product of the eval workstream.

## How it works + one small example

Collect questions from logs. Attach the schema version. Write expected SQL or expected result sets. Tag difficulty and dialect. Two labelers on a sample. Freeze a core.

Do not let the candidate model write the gold SQL.

## Failure modes

1. **Gold written by the model under test.**

2. **No schema version, so the gold rots.**

3. **Only happy-path SELECTs.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I build a custom set with real inputs, versioned schemas, independent gold, and tags. The candidate does not write the answers.

## A concrete walk-through

You take 80 warehouse questions, pin schema v3, and store expected result hashes. A model that writes pretty SQL that returns the wrong table fails.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about execution vs string-match SQL. Prefer execution / result hash.

## What I would measure

Label agreement, schema-version freshness, hard-case share.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Label agreement, schema-version freshness, hard-case share. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Real inputs + versioned context (schema). If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: I build a custom set with real inputs, versioned schemas, independent gold, and tags. The candidate does not write the answers. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about execution vs string-match SQL. Prefer execution / result hash. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Independent gold.
keyPoints: Stratify real inputs and include hard and out-of-scope cases
Measure labeller agreement and keep a held-out split

questions.q: How do you build a trustworthy custom eval dataset?
questions.a: Source real inputs, stratify across categories and difficulty, include hard and out-of-scope cases, label with a written guide and check agreement, keep a held-out test split, anonymise data and version everything.

questions.q: Your labels were generated by the same model you are evaluating. What is the problem?
questions.a: The reference favours that model's style and errors, biasing scores in its favour and hiding its mistakes. Use human or independent, verified labels, at least on a sample.

questions.q: How do you avoid biased references in a custom dataset?
questions.a: Human or independently verified labels with a guide — not the candidate model.

questions.q: For Text-to-SQL, what is a better check than string-equal SQL?
questions.a: Execute and compare result sets (or hashes) on a pinned schema.

questions.q: The schema changed and gold still passes. Risk?
questions.a: You are scoring against a dead world. Version the schema.

questions.q: What tags help?
questions.a: Difficulty, dialect, empty-result, adversarial.

like-for-like-model-comparison.explain:
## What it is

A comparison is only fair when everything except the model is held constant.

- Same **dataset** and same scoring method and judge.
- Same **prompt**, or a prompt tuned fairly for each model (budget equal effort); a prompt tuned for one model disadvantages others.
- Same **sampling settings** (temperature, max tokens), or each model at its recommended setting, documented.
- Same **retrieval and tools**.
- **Repeat runs** to measure variance.
- Pin **exact model versions** and record dates.
- Measure the same **cost and latency** definitions.

Report per-category results with intervals, not only a mean. If differences are inside run-to-run noise, say the models are tied on quality and let cost and latency decide.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Like-for-like means the same inputs, prompts, parameters, tools and scorer. A prompt hand-tuned for one candidate is a rigged race. Pin versions. Repeat if noisy.

Interviews: name what you held constant.

## How it works + one small example

One harness. One case file. Same temperature and tool list unless the product will differ on purpose (then say so). Repeat n=3 if the delta is small. Report CIs or at least min/max.

If you later tune a prompt per model, that is a second experiment, not the bake-off.

## Failure modes

1. **A prompt tuned only for the favourite.**

2. **Different tool schemas per model by accident.**

3. **Declaring a 0.5-point win inside noise.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Like-for-like holds inputs, prompts, tools and the scorer constant. A hand-tuned prompt is a different experiment. I do not ship a delta inside noise.

## A concrete walk-through

Two models differ by 0.4 on 80 cases. You repeat twice; they overlap. You pick the cheaper one. The favourite’s custom prompt is tried later as a second test.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about model-specific system prompts. Allowed in a second round, labelled as such.

## What I would measure

Constants listed in the report, deltas inside noise shipped (0).

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Constants listed in the report, deltas inside noise shipped (0). That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Same inputs, prompts, tools, scorer. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: Like-for-like holds inputs, prompts, tools and the scorer constant. A hand-tuned prompt is a different experiment. I do not ship a delta inside noise. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about model-specific system prompts. Allowed in a second round, labelled as such. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Pin model versions.
keyPoints: Per-model prompt tune is a second experiment.
Hold dataset, prompt effort, settings and tools constant
Repeat runs and report variance and per-slice results

questions.q: What must be held constant in a model comparison?
questions.a: Dataset, scoring method and judge, prompts (or equal tuning effort), sampling settings, retrieval and tools, exact model versions, and cost/latency definitions, with repeated runs to estimate noise.

questions.q: Model B loses to A but your prompt was written while testing A. What do you do?
questions.a: Give B an equal tuning effort or use a neutral prompt, then rerun. Otherwise the comparison reflects prompt fit, not model ability.

questions.q: In a like-for-like comparison, which is a flaw?
questions.a: Using a prompt hand-tuned only for one candidate.

questions.q: Two models differ by 0.5 within run noise. Decision?
questions.a: Treat as tied on quality and use cost/latency.

questions.q: What must you pin?
questions.a: Model id/version, prompt, tools, temperature, scorer version.

questions.q: When may prompts differ?
questions.a: In a labelled second experiment after the fair bake-off.

estimating-usage-token-cost.explain:
## What it is

Cost per request = input tokens x input price + output tokens x output price (check current provider pricing). Estimate with real data:

1. Measure the **average and tail** token counts of prompts: system prompt, retrieved context, history, user message, and outputs.
2. Multiply by **expected request volume** per day.
3. Add multipliers: retries, judge calls, multi-step agent loops, embeddings, and reasoning tokens for reasoning models.
4. Consider **caching** discounts for repeated prefixes, batch pricing, and cheaper routing.

Illustrative: 3,000 input and 500 output tokens at 10,000 requests per day gives 30M input and 5M output tokens daily; multiply by your prices. Output tokens usually cost more than input, and long context or agent loops dominate bills. Always size the p95 request, not just the average.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Quality without a cost model is a hobby. Estimate tokens in/out, calls per task (agents multiply), cache hits, and $ at your volume. Interviews: multiply by expected calls, including the tail.

## How it works + one small example

Log tokens per request. For agents, multiply by expected steps (p50 and p95). Apply list prices and any cache discount. Build a monthly $ at last week’s volume plus a 2× stress.

Prompt cache only helps if the prefix is stable. Say so.

## Failure modes

1. **Pricing a single call when the agent averages six.**

2. **Ignoring the p95 step count.**

3. **Forgetting output tokens.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I estimate $ from tokens × calls per task, including the tail. Agents multiply. Cache is a column, not a miracle.

## A concrete walk-through

A loop averages 6 calls; p95 is 14. Single-call pricing was $0.04; real p95 is $0.55. Finance sees the second number before launch.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about batch. Fine for offline eval, not for the user path unless you designed it.

## What I would measure

Predicted vs actual $, p95 calls used in the model.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Predicted vs actual $, p95 calls used in the model. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Tokens in and out, both. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: I estimate $ from tokens × calls per task, including the tail. Agents multiply. Cache is a column, not a miracle. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about batch. Fine for offline eval, not for the user path unless you designed it. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Multiply by calls per task.
keyPoints: Use p95, not only the mean.
Cache only if the prefix is stable.
Cost = tokens in and out times price, times volume
Include retries, agents, judges and reasoning tokens

questions.q: How would you estimate monthly LLM cost for a feature?
questions.a: Measure real input and output token counts per request including system prompt and retrieved context, multiply by prices and expected volume, add retries, agent steps and reasoning tokens, then account for caching or batch discounts and tail requests.

questions.q: Your estimate used average prompt size but the bill is double. Why?
questions.a: Long-tail requests with big contexts, chat history growth, retries and multi-step agent loops, or reasoning tokens were not counted. Use percentile sizes and trace-measured tokens.

questions.q: An agent loop makes about 6 calls per task. How does this affect cost estimation?
questions.a: Multiply per-call token use by expected calls, including tail cases.

questions.q: Why include output tokens?
questions.a: They are often pricier and grow with “helpful” verbosity.

questions.q: When does prompt cache change the estimate?
questions.a: When a long static prefix is actually reused. Otherwise it is a footnote.

questions.q: You priced the median and blew the bill. Why?
questions.a: The tail step-count dominates spend. Price p95 too.

quality-latency-cost-trade-off.explain:
## What it is

Every deployment chooses a point on three axes: **quality**, **latency** and **cost**. Usually you can have two cheaply.

- Larger models improve quality but raise cost and latency.
- Reasoning models spend extra tokens thinking: better on hard tasks, slower and costlier.
- Smaller models are fast and cheap but may fail hard cases.

Tactics: **route** easy queries to a cheap model and hard ones to a strong one, **cache** repeated prompts, shorten context, stream output to improve perceived latency, and use a cascade with escalation on low confidence.

Decide by the product: a chat UI needs fast first token; a nightly batch can use slower, cheaper settings; a high-stakes task prioritises quality. Express the trade-off as a table of quality score, p95 latency and cost per 1,000 requests for each candidate.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

The decision is a trade-off, not a max-quality trophy. A 0.5-point win at 3× cost and 2× p95 may be a loss. Interviews: three columns and a budget.

## How it works + one small example

Table: quality, p95 latency, $ / success. Mark the budget lines. Pick the cheapest that clears quality and latency. Consider routing: cheap default, escalate hard cases.

Ship the table, not a winner speech.

## Failure modes

1. **Max quality at any cost.**

2. **Ignoring latency because “it’s async” when it is not.**

3. **No routing even when the curve screams for it.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I pick the best quality/latency/cost point that clears the budget, not the trophy model. Routing is how I keep the cheap default.

## A concrete walk-through

Model A: +2 quality, 2× p95, 3× $. Budget is 1.2s p95. You ship B and route 8% to A. The table is in the design doc.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about “best model.” You ask “on which column.”

## What I would measure

Launches with a three-column table, routed share.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Launches with a three-column table, routed share. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Three columns: quality, latency, cost. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: I pick the best quality/latency/cost point that clears the budget, not the trophy model. Routing is how I keep the cheap default. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about “best model.” You ask “on which column.” I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Budgets are lines on the table.

## What would change my mind

The decision is a trade-off, not a max-quality trophy. A 0.5-point win at 3× cost and 2× p95 may be a loss. Interviews: three columns and a budget. I change the design when a held-out slice moves, not when a demo is prettier. A third point that would force a redesign is: Trophy quality can lose. One counter-example that lives in the golden set beats a week of vibe testing.
keyPoints: Budgets are lines on the table.
Larger or reasoning models raise quality, cost and latency together
Routing, caching and cascades move you along the frontier

questions.q: How do you choose between a strong slow model and a cheap fast one?
questions.a: Quantify quality, p95 latency and cost per request for both on your eval, compare to product requirements (UX latency, error cost, budget), and consider routing easy requests to the cheap model with escalation for hard ones.

questions.q: Name techniques that improve cost or latency without changing the model.
questions.a: Prompt/context shortening, prompt caching of stable prefixes, response caching, batching, streaming for perceived latency, output length limits, and routing or cascades.

questions.q: Two models are tied on quality; one is 3× cheaper. Reasonable decision?
questions.a: Treat as tied on quality and choose the cheaper if latency is acceptable.

questions.q: A +2 quality at 2× p95 misses the latency budget. Ship it?
questions.a: Not unless product moves the budget. Consider routing instead.

questions.q: What is routing here?
questions.a: Send easy cases to a cheap model and escalate hard ones.

questions.q: Why “per success” not “per call”?
questions.a: Failed or retried calls still cost. Success is what the user bought.

stratify-the-custom-set.explain:
## What it is

**Easy, hard, adversarial, and the last five production misses.** A custom set that is all easy twins will score 98% and lie. Stratify on purpose so a model cannot hide on the happy path.

The last five misses keep the set honest this week.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interview closer for custom sets. They want the strata names. On the job this is how you stop a vanity 98%.

## How it works + one small example

Quota: 40% typical, 25% hard, 20% adversarial (injection, empty, dialect), 15% recent misses (rotating). Report scores by stratum, not only overall.

When a miss ages out of “recent,” it can stay in hard.

## Failure modes

1. **All easy.**

2. **Adversarial only, so you never see typical quality.**

3. **Overall average hiding a dead adversarial slice.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I stratify easy, hard, adversarial, and recent misses. I report by slice. A 98% overall on easy twins is a lie.

## A concrete walk-through

Overall 91%, adversarial 40%. You stop celebrating. A prompt change lifts adversarial to 70% and overall only +2. That was the win.

## Interview follow-up

They ask how many adversarial. Enough to see a number, not 3 cases.

## What I would measure

Stratum sizes, overall-only reports retired.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Stratum sizes, overall-only reports retired. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Quota the strata; do not hope. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: I stratify easy, hard, adversarial, and recent misses. I report by slice. A 98% overall on easy twins is a lie. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask how many adversarial. Enough to see a number, not 3 cases. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Include recent misses.

## What would change my mind

Interview closer for custom sets. They want the strata names. On the job this is how you stop a vanity 98%. I change the design when a held-out slice moves, not when a demo is prettier. A third point that would force a redesign is: Report by slice. One counter-example that lives in the golden set beats a week of vibe testing.

## How this shows up in a log

In a real trace I want to see the decision, the evidence, and the stop. A reviewer should be able to replay this walk-through from the log: Overall 91%, adversarial 40%. You stop celebrating. A prompt change lifts adversarial to 70% and overall only +2. That was the win. If the log cannot support that story, the feature is not observable yet. I also want the cheap how-it-works sketch nearby so a new teammate can implement the same check: Quota: 40% typical, 25% hard, 20% adversarial (injection, empty, dialect), 15% recent misses (rotating). Report scores by stratum, not only overall. When a miss ages out of “recent,” it can stay in hard.
keyPoints: Quota the strata; do not hope.

questions.q: How should you stratify a custom eval set?
questions.a: Easy, hard, adversarial, and the last production misses — with quotas and per-slice scores.

questions.q: Overall 98% on easy twins. What is missing?
questions.a: Hard, adversarial and recent-miss strata.

questions.q: What happens to an old “recent miss”?
questions.a: It stays in hard or typical; the recent bucket rotates.

questions.q: Why report by slice?
questions.a: Wins and losses offset in the average.

questions.q: How many adversarial cases?
questions.a: Enough to estimate a rate — dozens, not three.

cost-model-beside-the-quality-table.explain:
## What it is

**Tokens and latency are columns, not footnotes.** The quality table that ships a model without $ and p95 is unfinished. Put the columns in the same grid so a 1-point win cannot hide a 4× bill.

This is the trade-off topic as a documentation rule.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interview close: they show a quality-only slide. You ask for the other columns. On the job, finance will.

## How it works + one small example

Every bake-off artefact: quality | p95 ms | $ / 1k tasks | notes. Fill them even if estimated. Update with actuals after a week.

If a cell is “unknown,” the table is not done.

## Failure modes

1. **Quality-only slides to leadership.**

2. **Cost in a buried appendix.**

3. **Latency measured on a laptop Wi-Fi and treated as p95.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Tokens and latency are columns on the same table as quality. If a cell is empty, the bake-off is not done.

## A concrete walk-through

You add the columns. The “winner” is 4× $ . Leadership picks the second row. That is the table working.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about carbon or energy. Fine as another column if the org cares; do not let it replace $.

## What I would measure

Bake-offs with all three columns, appendix-only costs (0).

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Bake-offs with all three columns, appendix-only costs (0). That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Quality, latency, $ in one grid. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: Tokens and latency are columns on the same table as quality. If a cell is empty, the bake-off is not done. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about carbon or energy. Fine as another column if the org cares; do not let it replace $. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Empty cell = unfinished.

## What would change my mind

Interview close: they show a quality-only slide. You ask for the other columns. On the job, finance will. I change the design when a held-out slice moves, not when a demo is prettier. A third point that would force a redesign is: No buried appendix. One counter-example that lives in the golden set beats a week of vibe testing.

## How this shows up in a log

In a real trace I want to see the decision, the evidence, and the stop. A reviewer should be able to replay this walk-through from the log: You add the columns. The “winner” is 4× $ . Leadership picks the second row. That is the table working. If the log cannot support that story, the feature is not observable yet. I also want the cheap how-it-works sketch nearby so a new teammate can implement the same check: Every bake-off artefact: quality | p95 ms | $ / 1k tasks | notes. Fill them even if estimated. Update with actuals after a week. If a cell is “unknown,” the table is not done.

questions.q: What columns sit beside quality in a bake-off table?
questions.a: Latency (p95) and cost (tokens / $ per success).

questions.q: The winner slide has only quality. What do you ask?
questions.a: For p95 and $ / 1k tasks on the same rows.

questions.q: Laptop latency as p95 — problem?
questions.a: It is not production p95. Measure on the real path.

questions.q: When is the table done?
questions.a: When no required cell is unknown.

questions.q: Why not bury cost in an appendix?
questions.a: It will not change the decision if nobody sees it next to quality.

component-pipeline-application-levels.explain:
## What it is

Evaluate at three levels:

- **Component**: one piece in isolation, such as a retriever, a classifier prompt, a tool, or a parser. Fast, cheap, precise for locating faults.
- **Pipeline**: several components chained, e.g. retrieve then generate, to find interaction problems.
- **Application (end-to-end)**: the whole product from user input to final behaviour, including UI-visible output, latency and cost.

Why all three: end-to-end tells you *that* quality dropped, component tests tell you *where*. A pipeline can fail while each component passes (good retrieval, but the generator ignores it). Build many cheap component tests, fewer pipeline tests and a small set of end-to-end tests, like the test pyramid in software.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Structure evals at component, pipeline and application levels. Component: retriever or generator alone. Pipeline: retrieve→generate. Application: user-visible plus tone, format, ops.

A drop should be localisable in one dashboard hop.

## How it works + one small example

Same ids across levels. A case has component scores and an application score. When e2e drops, read the components. When components are green and e2e is red, inspect assembly.

Do not maintain three unrelated spreadsheets.

## Failure modes

1. **Only application.**

2. **Components with different case ids.**

3. **Pipeline skipped so you never see assembly bugs.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I score component, pipeline and application on the same cases. That is how I localise a drop in one hop.

## A concrete walk-through

Application −5, retriever flat, generator-on-gold −6. You fix the prompt. The shared ids made the hop obvious.

## Interview follow-up

They ask RAGAS vs DeepEval. Either can run a level; you still own the structure.

## What I would measure

Time-to-localise, shared-id coverage.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Time-to-localise, shared-id coverage. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Three levels: component, pipeline, application. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: I score component, pipeline and application on the same cases. That is how I localise a drop in one hop. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask RAGAS vs DeepEval. Either can run a level; you still own the structure. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Shared case ids.

## What would change my mind

Structure evals at component, pipeline and application levels. Component: retriever or generator alone. Pipeline: retrieve→generate. Application: user-visible plus tone, format, ops. A drop should be localisable in one dashboard hop. I change the design when a held-out slice moves, not when a demo is prettier. A third point that would force a redesign is: E2E drop → read components. One counter-example that lives in the golden set beats a week of vibe testing.
keyPoints: Component tests locate faults; end-to-end tests detect user impact
Components can pass while the pipeline fails

questions.q: Why test components, pipelines and the whole application?
questions.a: End-to-end shows user-visible regressions, but component tests isolate the cause cheaply and pipeline tests catch interaction failures. A pyramid gives speed and diagnosability.

questions.q: End-to-end score fell but you do not know why. What is your approach?
questions.a: Run component evals (retriever, generator, tools) on the same cases to see which regressed, then pipeline tests to check interactions, and read failing traces.

questions.q: A RAG app’s e2e score dropped. Fastest localisation?
questions.a: Run retriever and generator component evals on the same cases.

questions.q: What does the pipeline level add?
questions.a: The retrieve→context→generate interaction, not just isolated parts.

questions.q: Different case ids per level — problem?
questions.a: You cannot join a drop. Share ids.

questions.q: Where do tone and p95 live?
questions.a: Application level, next to correctness.

versioning-tests-configs-results.explain:
## What it is

To compare runs reliably, version **everything** that affects a score:

- **Tests**: dataset version, labelling guide, scoring code and judge prompt.
- **Configs**: model name and exact version, prompts, temperature, retrieval parameters, tool definitions, code commit.
- **Results**: raw outputs, scores, traces, cost and latency, timestamps.

Store these together as an immutable **run record**, tying a score to the exact inputs. Use git for prompts and datasets, content hashes for files, and an experiment store for results. Without this, you cannot reproduce a number, tell if a change or a data edit moved the score, or audit a release decision. Changing the dataset or judge resets comparability, so bump versions and re-baseline.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

If you cannot reproduce a number, you do not have science. Version cases, prompts, models, configs and results together. A folder of scores without hashes is folklore.

Interviews: what you store per run.

## How it works + one small example

Each run record: dataset hash, prompt hash, model id, params, scorer version, outputs, scores, git sha. Immutable. Compare by id, not by “Thursday’s run.”

Prompts in git. Results in an artefact store.

## Failure modes

1. **Overwriting last week’s outputs.**

2. **Prompts only in the UI.**

3. **A spreadsheet with no hashes.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I version cases, prompts, models, configs and results. A score without those hashes is folklore. I can reproduce last month’s number.

## A concrete walk-through

A stakeholder asks why June was 81. You open run `2026-06-12-a` with hashes and outputs. The argument ends.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about DVC or a vendor. Fine. The fields matter more than the brand.

## What I would measure

Repro success rate, overwritten runs (0).

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Repro success rate, overwritten runs (0). That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Hash dataset, prompt, model, params, scorer. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: I version cases, prompts, models, configs and results. A score without those hashes is folklore. I can reproduce last month’s number. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about DVC or a vendor. Fine. The fields matter more than the brand. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Immutable run records.

## What would change my mind

If you cannot reproduce a number, you do not have science. Version cases, prompts, models, configs and results together. A folder of scores without hashes is folklore. Interviews: what you store per run. I change the design when a held-out slice moves, not when a demo is prettier. A third point that would force a redesign is: Prompts in git. One counter-example that lives in the golden set beats a week of vibe testing.
keyPoints: Hash dataset, prompt, model, params, scorer.
Version datasets, scoring code, prompts, model and settings
Store immutable run records linking score to configuration

questions.q: What must be versioned to make eval results reproducible?
questions.a: Dataset and labels, scoring code and judge prompt, model version, prompts, parameters, retrieval and tool configs, code commit, and the raw outputs and scores of each run.

questions.q: Scores jumped 6 points overnight with no prompt change. How could versioning help?
questions.a: Run records would show whether dataset, judge, model version or settings changed. If the dataset or judge changed, the scores are not comparable and need re-baselining.

questions.q: What is essential to reproduce a score weeks later?
questions.a: Immutable run records with dataset, prompt, model version and settings.

questions.q: Thursday’s spreadsheet is gone. What failed?
questions.a: You overwrote or never stored hashes. Use immutable artefacts.

questions.q: Where do prompts live?
questions.a: In git, hashed into the run record.

questions.q: May you mutate gold in place?
questions.a: No. Version it. Old runs need the old gold.

experiment-tracking-baselines.explain:
## What it is

**Experiment tracking** logs each eval run (configuration, metrics, outputs) so runs can be compared. A **baseline** is a reference run, typically current production, against which every change is judged.

Practice:
- Always compare a candidate to the baseline on the *same* dataset version.
- Change one thing at a time or log all changes clearly.
- Report per-slice deltas and variance, not only the mean.
- Look at individual flipped cases (pass to fail, fail to pass), not just totals; a flat average can hide offsetting wins and losses.
- Promote a candidate to the new baseline only after approval.

Tools such as MLflow, Weights & Biases, LangSmith, Braintrust or Langfuse provide tracking; the discipline matters more than the tool.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

An experiment without a baseline is a vibe. Track runs and always diff the last shipped (or last accepted) baseline. Look at flipped cases, not only the average.

Interviews: what a baseline is.

## How it works + one small example

Baseline = last shipped config’s scores on the frozen core. Each experiment: delta overall, delta by slice, list of flips. A +1 average with −20 on refunds is a fail.

Name the baseline id in the PR.

## Failure modes

1. **No baseline.**

2. **Average-only diffs.**

3. **Moving the baseline to the favourite run.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I diff every experiment to a named baseline and I read flipped cases. Averages can hide a dead slice.

## A concrete walk-through

+0.8 overall, 12 refund flips to fail. You do not ship. The flip list is the artefact.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about multiple baselines. One shipped, one “best so far” is OK if labelled.

## What I would measure

PRs with baseline ids, average-only reports retired.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: PRs with baseline ids, average-only reports retired. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Baseline = last shipped on the frozen core. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: I diff every experiment to a named baseline and I read flipped cases. Averages can hide a dead slice. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about multiple baselines. One shipped, one “best so far” is OK if labelled. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Diff averages and flips.

## What would change my mind

An experiment without a baseline is a vibe. Track runs and always diff the last shipped (or last accepted) baseline. Look at flipped cases, not only the average. Interviews: what a baseline is. I change the design when a held-out slice moves, not when a demo is prettier. A third point that would force a redesign is: Name the baseline in the PR. One counter-example that lives in the golden set beats a week of vibe testing.
keyPoints: Baseline = last shipped on the frozen core.
Name the baseline in the PR.
A +1 with a dead slice is a fail.
Compare to a baseline on the same dataset version
Inspect flipped cases and per-slice deltas

questions.q: Why look at flipped cases rather than the average only?
questions.a: A flat average can hide improvements in some cases offset by regressions in others. Flipped pass-to-fail cases reveal what broke so you can judge risk.

questions.q: You tuned prompt, model and retrieval simultaneously and the score rose. What is the issue?
questions.a: You cannot attribute the gain or know which change might hurt elsewhere. Vary one factor at a time or run controlled ablations against the baseline.

questions.q: Why can an unchanged average still hide a problem?
questions.a: Wins and regressions can offset across cases or slices. Read flips.

questions.q: What is the baseline?
questions.a: The last shipped prompt/model/config scores on the frozen core.

questions.q: A PR with +1 overall and a dead refund slice. Ship?
questions.a: No. The slice is a gate.

questions.q: Who may move the baseline?
questions.a: A shipped (or explicitly accepted) run, not a favourite notebook.

ci-cd-quality-gates.explain:
## What it is

A **quality gate** blocks a merge or deploy if eval results fall below a threshold, bringing software discipline to LLM changes.

Design:
- **Fast tier on every PR**: a small smoke set with cheap programmatic checks and a limited judge budget.
- **Full tier on main or nightly**: the larger set, repeated runs.
- **Thresholds**: absolute minimums (e.g. safety 100%, format 99%) and relative (no category drops more than a set margin versus baseline).
- **Hard gates for critical rules**, soft warnings for noisy metrics.
- Surface a report with failing cases in the PR.

Handle flakiness through repeats and tolerance bands; otherwise people learn to ignore the gate. Keep cost in check with sampling and caching of unchanged cases.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

A quality gate fails the build when important metrics regress. Without it, evals are optional homework. With a naive gate, one flake blocks the company.

Design: smoke on PR, full nightly, thresholds with tolerance.

## How it works + one small example

PR: 20 cheap programmatic cases, fail on format or P0 slice. Nightly: full suite vs baseline, fail on a meaningful drop (e.g. −3 overall or −5 on P0) after a repeat.

Never fail on a single stochastic case. Pin the scorer.

## Failure modes

1. **No gate.**

2. **Full expensive suite on every commit.**

3. **Gate on a judge you just changed.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

CI fails on a meaningful, repeated drop — not on one flake. Smoke on PRs, full nightly. The gate is how evals become real.

## A concrete walk-through

A prompt PR fails smoke (JSON). You fix in minutes. Nightly catches a −4 refund slice. That is the gate working at two speeds.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about skip. Emergencies skip with a ticket, not by deleting the gate.

## What I would measure

Gates that fired correctly, flake fails, skipped emergencies.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Gates that fired correctly, flake fails, skipped emergencies. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Gates make evals real. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: CI fails on a meaningful, repeated drop — not on one flake. Smoke on PRs, full nightly. The gate is how evals become real. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about skip. Emergencies skip with a ticket, not by deleting the gate. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Smoke on PR, full nightly.

## What would change my mind

A quality gate fails the build when important metrics regress. Without it, evals are optional homework. With a naive gate, one flake blocks the company. Design: smoke on PR, full nightly, thresholds with tolerance. I change the design when a held-out slice moves, not when a demo is prettier. A third point that would force a redesign is: Thresholds with tolerance. One counter-example that lives in the golden set beats a week of vibe testing.
keyPoints: Do not gate on a just-changed judge.
Fast smoke tier on PRs, full suite nightly or on main
Use absolute and relative thresholds; hard gates for critical rules

questions.q: How do you design CI quality gates for an LLM app?
questions.a: A small fast smoke set on each PR and a full suite on main or nightly, with absolute thresholds for critical behaviours and relative no-regression margins versus baseline, reports showing failing cases, and repeats to tame flakiness.

questions.q: The CI eval gate fails randomly and developers start bypassing it. Fix?
questions.a: Reduce variance with repeated runs, pinned versions and temperature, widen tolerance on noisy metrics, make critical checks deterministic, and only hard-fail on stable metrics.

questions.q: Which CI design best limits cost while protecting quality?
questions.a: Smoke set on PRs, full suite nightly, thresholds with tolerance.

questions.q: A single case flakes and blocks main. Fix?
questions.a: Require a repeated drop or a slice threshold, not one stochastic fail.

questions.q: May you skip the gate in an incident?
questions.a: With an explicit ticket and a follow-up run — not by deleting it.

questions.q: What must be pinned in CI?
questions.a: Model id (or a mock), dataset hash, scorer version.

self-improving-golden-dataset.explain:
## What it is

A **self-improving golden dataset** grows from real usage instead of being frozen.

Loop:
1. Production traces and feedback surface failures, low scores and novel queries.
2. A reviewer (or judge plus spot check) labels them.
3. Approved cases are added with a version bump.
4. The next releases are tested against the richer set.

Guardrails: dedupe and cluster so common patterns do not dominate; keep a **frozen held-out core** for stable trend lines and a separate growing set; record when each case was added so score changes can be explained; strip PII; avoid training or prompt-tuning on the held-out part. Prune obsolete cases when the product changes. The risk is quiet drift where the dataset stops matching the earlier baseline, so always re-score the baseline on the new version.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

The set improves when prod failures and new edges enter it — with a frozen core so you cannot game the trend. Interviews: living set + frozen core.

Self-improving is not automatic labelling by the model under test.

## How it works + one small example

Two pools: core (frozen, trend) and growth (adds from prod). Periodically promote growth into a new core version. Never let the candidate label gold.

A monthly review retires outdated cases (policy changed).

## Failure modes

1. **Only growth, no frozen core.**

2. **Model-labelled gold.**

3. **Never retiring dead policies.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

The golden set grows from prod misses and keeps a frozen core for trends. The candidate does not write gold. Dead policies retire.

## A concrete walk-through

Core 80 is stable. Growth added 40 this quarter. You cut a v2 core of 100 and keep 20 as extra. Trends remain comparable.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about synthetic. OK as growth if humans review; still not the frozen core on day one.

## What I would measure

Adds from prod, core stability, retired dead cases.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Adds from prod, core stability, retired dead cases. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Frozen core + growth pool. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: The golden set grows from prod misses and keeps a frozen core for trends. The candidate does not write gold. Dead policies retire. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about synthetic. OK as growth if humans review; still not the frozen core on day one. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Adds from prod misses.
keyPoints: Promote versions, do not mutate silently.
Production failures and new queries are labelled and added
Keep a frozen held-out core plus a growing set

questions.q: How does a golden dataset improve itself over time?
questions.a: Failures and novel production queries are sampled, labelled by reviewers and added with versioning, deduped and balanced, so the set tracks real use. A frozen core preserves comparable trends.

questions.q: Why re-score the baseline after adding cases?
questions.a: The new dataset changes the score scale; a candidate versus an old-baseline number would not be comparable. Re-running the baseline on the same version keeps comparisons fair.

questions.q: What does a frozen held-out core provide?
questions.a: Stable trend lines across releases that you cannot tune against.

questions.q: Who must not write the new gold labels?
questions.a: The model under test.

questions.q: Policy changed; old cases still fail. What do you do?
questions.a: Retire or rewrite them. Do not keep a dead policy as a fail.

questions.q: How do you grow without ruining trends?
questions.a: Add to a growth pool; periodically version a new core.

quality-alongside-latency-cost.explain:
## What it is

Quality scores alone can approve a change that doubles latency or cost. Track **quality, latency and cost together** in every eval run.

- Record tokens, dollar cost, time to first token and total latency per case.
- Gate on all three: for example, quality must not drop more than a set margin, p95 latency below a limit, and cost per request below a budget.
- Show a Pareto view of candidates: a change is only clearly better if it improves one axis without hurting others.

Example (illustrative): prompt v2 adds few-shot examples, quality +2 points, input tokens x2, latency +30%. Whether that is worth it depends on the budget; the data lets you decide explicitly.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

A quality gate that ignores p95 and $ will ship a gorgeous brick. Track the three together in CI and in weekly review. A +2 with doubled p95 needs a product yes.

## How it works + one small example

The nightly job records quality, p95, $ / 1k. The gate can fail on any budget. The weekly mail is one table.

Optimising one column in isolation is how you get 8k-token answers that score well and time out.

## Failure modes

1. **Quality-only gates.**

2. **Latency measured only in the app, never in the eval job.**

3. **Celebrating +2 with a timeout spike.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I track quality next to latency and cost in the same gate. A quality win that blows p95 does not ship without a budget change.

## A concrete walk-through

Nightly: +2 quality, p95 2.1s vs 1.0s budget. The gate fails. You shorten the prompt instead of arguing.

## Interview follow-up

They ask which column wins. The written budget wins.

## What I would measure

Gates failed on latency/$, quality-only ships (0).

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Gates failed on latency/$, quality-only ships (0). That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Three columns in CI and in the weekly mail. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: I track quality next to latency and cost in the same gate. A quality win that blows p95 does not ship without a budget change. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask which column wins. The written budget wins. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Any budget can fail the gate.

## What would change my mind

A quality gate that ignores p95 and $ will ship a gorgeous brick. Track the three together in CI and in weekly review. A +2 with doubled p95 needs a product yes. I change the design when a held-out slice moves, not when a demo is prettier. A third point that would force a redesign is: Do not celebrate +2 with a timeout. One counter-example that lives in the golden set beats a week of vibe testing.
keyPoints: Three columns in CI and in the weekly mail.
Any budget can fail the gate.
Do not celebrate +2 with a timeout.
Measure latency on the real path.
Log tokens, cost and latency in every eval run
Gate on quality, p95 latency and cost together

questions.q: Why include latency and cost in eval runs?
questions.a: A change that improves quality may unacceptably raise latency or cost; tracking all three exposes trade-offs and lets gates enforce budgets.

questions.q: A prompt change gives +1 quality point and 40% more tokens. How decide?
questions.a: Compare against budget and latency limits and the value of the point on critical slices; accept if within budget or if gains concentrate on high-value cases, else look for shorter prompts or caching.

questions.q: A change raises quality 2 points but p95 latency doubles. Response?
questions.a: Check the latency budget; mitigate or reject. Do not ship on quality alone.

questions.q: Why measure latency in the eval job too?
questions.a: So the gate sees it. App-only metrics can lag or miss the candidate path.

questions.q: Who wins if columns conflict?
questions.a: The written budget — product/finance lines, not the researcher’s favourite column.

questions.q: A verbose answer scores well and times out. Verdict?
questions.a: A cost/latency fail even if the rubric is happy.

a-quality-gate-in-ci.explain:
## What it is

**Fail the build on a statistically meaningful drop, not on one flaky case.** That is the gate rule. Meaningful means a threshold you chose (overall or P0 slice) and, for stochastic scores, a repeat.

A gate that never fails is décor. A gate that always flakes will be deleted.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

The CI closer. Interviews: how you avoid both rubber stamps and flake hell.

## How it works + one small example

Config: `fail_if overall_delta <= -3 or refund_delta <= -5`. Stochastic: run twice, fail if both miss. Publish the rule in the README.

Review monthly whether the thresholds still match product risk.

## Failure modes

1. **Threshold 0 on a 20-case stochastic set.**

2. **No P0 slice rule.**

3. **A gate nobody can explain.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

The build fails on a meaningful, repeated drop. One flake is not a fail. A gate I cannot explain will be deleted.

## A concrete walk-through

You set −3/−5 with a repeat. Flake tickets die. A real refund regression still fails. The rule is in the README.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about Bayesian tests. Fine later; a simple repeated threshold ships first.

## What I would measure

Flake-fail rate, real regressions caught, README clarity.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Flake-fail rate, real regressions caught, README clarity. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Meaningful threshold, not one case. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: The build fails on a meaningful, repeated drop. One flake is not a fail. A gate I cannot explain will be deleted. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about Bayesian tests. Fine later; a simple repeated threshold ships first. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Repeat stochastic scores.

## What would change my mind

The CI closer. Interviews: how you avoid both rubber stamps and flake hell. I change the design when a held-out slice moves, not when a demo is prettier. A third point that would force a redesign is: P0 slices can fail alone. One counter-example that lives in the golden set beats a week of vibe testing.

In a real trace I want to see the decision, the evidence, and the stop. A reviewer should be able to replay this walk-through from the log: You set −3/−5 with a repeat. Flake tickets die. A real refund regression still fails. The rule is in the README. If the log cannot support that story, the feature is not observable yet. I also want the cheap how-it-works sketch nearby so a new teammate can implement the same check: Config: `fail_if overall_delta <= -3 or refund_delta <= -5`. Stochastic: run twice, fail if both miss. Publish the rule in the README. Review monthly whether the thresholds still match product risk.

four-levels-of-rag-evaluation.explain:
## What it is

RAG quality can be evaluated at four levels, each answering a different question:

1. **Retriever**: does it fetch the right chunks? (recall, precision, ranking)
2. **Generator**: given good context, does the model produce a faithful, useful answer?
3. **Pipeline**: do retrieval and generation work together end to end? (RAG Triad)
4. **System/behaviour**: quality from the user's view plus operational and safety concerns (correctness, completeness, tone, cost, PII, injection).

Evaluating only the final answer hides the cause of failures. Layered evaluation lets you say "the answer was wrong because the retriever missed the document" rather than "the answer was wrong". Start with retriever and generator in isolation, then add pipeline and system checks.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

RAG is four eval problems stacked: component (retriever, generator), pipeline (triad), application (user-facing correctness), and safety (injection, PII, jailbreak). Treating it as one black-box score hides the broken layer.

Interviews: draw the four and give one metric each.

## How it works + one small example

Dashboard with four rows. A wrong answer starts at application, then you drop a level until the cause appears. Safety is not optional because retrieved text is an attacker channel.

Keep case ids shared across levels.

## Failure modes

1. **One e2e number for the whole RAG system.**

2. **Safety left for “later.”**

3. **Components with different cases.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I eval RAG at component, pipeline, application and safety. A single black-box score cannot tell me which layer failed.

## A concrete walk-through

Users get a wrong rate. Application is down; triad shows low context relevance; retriever recall is the hole. You fix ingestion, not the prompt.

## Interview follow-up

They ask if RAGAS is the four levels. It is a library; you still own the structure.

## What I would measure

Drops localised to a level, safety cases present.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Drops localised to a level, safety cases present. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Four levels: component, pipeline, application, safety. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: I eval RAG at component, pipeline, application and safety. A single black-box score cannot tell me which layer failed. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask if RAGAS is the four levels. It is a library; you still own the structure. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Shared case ids.
keyPoints: Four levels: component, pipeline, application, safety.
Safety is required — retrieval is an attack channel.
One metric per level at minimum.
Libraries do not replace the structure.
Layering locates the cause of a bad answer

questions.q: Name the four levels of RAG evaluation and what each checks.
questions.a: Retriever (right chunks fetched), generator (faithful useful answer from good context), pipeline (components working together, e.g. RAG Triad), and system behaviour (user-facing correctness, tone, safety, cost).

questions.q: Why is final-answer-only evaluation inadequate for RAG?
questions.a: It cannot tell whether a failure came from missed retrieval, noisy context, an unfaithful generator or a prompt issue, so you do not know what to fix.

questions.q: Why not treat RAG as one black-box eval?
questions.a: Because a wrong answer can be retrieval, assembly, generation or safety. Levels localise.

questions.q: A wrong answer appears. How do you walk the levels?
questions.a: Application first, then pipeline triad, then the failing component, and check safety if the path is untrusted.

questions.q: Why is safety its own level for RAG?
questions.a: Retrieved documents can inject or leak. Component quality can be fine while safety fails.

questions.q: What must be shared across levels?
questions.a: Case ids so you can join a drop.

evaluating-the-retriever-alone.explain:
## What it is

Evaluate the retriever without the LLM: given a query, did it return the chunks that contain the answer?

Setup: a dataset of queries each with the **relevant document or chunk IDs** (the ground truth). Run only the retrieval step, and compare the top-k results to the ground truth with retrieval metrics.

Benefits: fast, deterministic, cheap (no generation), and directly tunes chunking, embedding model, hybrid search, top-k and reranking. A generator cannot answer correctly if the evidence is not retrieved, so retriever recall is an upper bound on answer quality for questions that need documents.

Vary one parameter at a time (chunk size, overlap, model, k) and watch the metrics.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

If the chunk is not there, the generator cannot be faithful to the truth. Retriever-alone eval asks: did we fetch what a labelled set says is needed? Do this before you tune the prompt again.

## How it works + one small example

Gold: query → chunk ids (or passages). Metrics: Recall@k, MRR, precision@k. Hold the generator out. Slice by corpus and query type.

A miss here is an index/query/chunking problem, not a temperature problem.

## Failure modes

1. **Only judging the final sentence.**

2. **Gold chunks that are just the question restated.**

3. **k chosen after looking at scores.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I eval the retriever alone on labelled query→chunk ids. If recall is dead, I do not touch the generator first.

## A concrete walk-through

Recall@5 is 0.41. You fix chunking and a filter. Generator-on-gold was already 0.88. E2E follows the recall lift.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about implicit gold. LLM-judged “is this relevant” is weaker than human ids; say so.

## What I would measure

Recall@k, MRR, generator held out.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Recall@k, MRR, generator held out. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Retriever-alone uses labelled chunk ids. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: I eval the retriever alone on labelled query→chunk ids. If recall is dead, I do not touch the generator first. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about implicit gold. LLM-judged “is this relevant” is weaker than human ids; say so. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Hold the generator out.

## What would change my mind

If the chunk is not there, the generator cannot be faithful to the truth. Retriever-alone eval asks: did we fetch what a labelled set says is needed? Do this before you tune the prompt again. I change the design when a held-out slice moves, not when a demo is prettier. A third point that would force a redesign is: Recall@k and MRR first. One counter-example that lives in the golden set beats a week of vibe testing.
keyPoints: Do not retune the prompt first.
Test retrieval alone against labelled relevant chunks
Fast, cheap and deterministic for tuning chunking and embeddings

questions.q: How do you evaluate a retriever independently of the LLM?
questions.a: Build queries with labelled relevant chunk IDs, run only retrieval, and compute metrics like recall@k, precision@k, MRR or nDCG. Tune chunking, embeddings, k and reranking.

questions.q: Why does retriever recall limit the whole RAG system?
questions.a: If the relevant evidence is not in the retrieved context, the generator cannot ground the answer, so it either refuses or hallucinates.

questions.q: A RAG answer is wrong. How do you identify a retriever fault?
questions.a: Eval the retriever on the same case against gold chunks. If they are missing, stop blaming the generator.

questions.q: What does retriever-alone need?
questions.a: A labelled query→chunk set and ranking metrics, with the generator held out.

questions.q: Gold chunks are paraphrases of the question. Risk?
questions.a: The set is too easy and lexical. Use independent labels.
