questions.a: So a fluent wrong answer cannot hide a miss.

diagnosing-missed-noisy-retrieval.explain:
## What it is

Two retrieval failures with different fixes:

- **Missed retrieval (low recall)**: the needed chunk is not returned. Causes: chunks too large or small, poor embedding match for jargon, query phrasing mismatch, k too low, metadata filters, missing content in the index. Fixes: better chunking, hybrid keyword+vector search, query rewriting or expansion, higher k followed by reranking, enrich index.
- **Noisy retrieval (low precision)**: relevant chunk is present but surrounded by irrelevant ones, distracting the generator or wasting tokens. Fixes: reranker, smaller k, score thresholds, better chunk boundaries, metadata filtering.

Diagnose by inspecting retrieved lists for failing queries: is the right chunk absent, ranked low, or buried in junk? Rank position matters because models attend less to the middle of long contexts.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Two failure shapes: miss (relevant chunk absent) and noise (too much junk in the window). They want opposite fixes. Interviews: diagnose before you raise k.

## How it works + one small example

For each fail: is the gold chunk in the index? in the top k? in the prompt after assembly? Miss-in-index → ingest. Miss-in-rank → rerank or k. Present-but-noisy → rerank and cut k.

A gold chunk at rank 14 with k=5 is a ranking problem.

## Failure modes

1. **Raising k on a miss-in-index.**

2. **Raising k on noise.**

3. **Not checking whether the chunk exists at all.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I diagnose miss versus noise. Missing from the index is ingest. Missing from top k is rank. Noise means cut and rerank, not raise k.

## A concrete walk-through

Gold is at rank 14. You retrieve 20 and rerank to 5. Recall@5 jumps. Raising k to 20 without rerank had made answers worse.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about hybrid search. It is a rank/ingest tool, not a generator tool.

## What I would measure

Miss-in-index vs miss-in-rank vs noise rates.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Miss-in-index vs miss-in-rank vs noise rates. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Miss vs noise are different bugs. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: I diagnose miss versus noise. Missing from the index is ingest. Missing from top k is rank. Noise means cut and rerank, not raise k. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about hybrid search. It is a rank/ingest tool, not a generator tool. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Check index, then rank, then assembly.
keyPoints: Miss vs noise are different bugs.
Check index, then rank, then assembly.
Do not raise k on noise.
Rank 14 with k=5 is a rerank problem.
Missed = recall problem; noisy = precision problem
Check absent vs low-ranked vs buried relevant chunk

questions.q: How do you distinguish missed from noisy retrieval?
questions.a: Look at retrieved lists for failing queries: if the relevant chunk is absent, it's a recall miss; if present but with many irrelevant chunks, it's noisy retrieval. Metrics: recall@k versus precision@k.

questions.q: Relevant chunk is at rank 12 and k=5. Fix options?
questions.a: Improve ranking with a reranker or hybrid search, or retrieve more candidates (say 20-50) and rerank to top 5. Also review query rewriting and chunking so the chunk scores higher.

questions.q: Relevant chunk at rank 14, k=5. Most direct fix?
questions.a: Retrieve more candidates and rerank, or add a reranker — the chunk exists.

questions.q: Most failures are “not in the index.” Best action?
questions.a: Fix ingestion and coverage. Downstream tuning cannot add missing docs.

questions.q: You raised k and answers got worse. Why?
questions.a: You added noise and buried the useful span.

questions.q: What three places can a gold chunk be missing?
questions.a: Index, top-k ranking, or the assembled prompt (truncated).

retrieval-metrics.explain:
## What it is

Standard retrieval metrics (computed against labelled relevant items):

- **Recall@k**: fraction of relevant items found in the top k. Key for RAG since missing evidence is fatal.
- **Precision@k**: fraction of the top k that are relevant. Measures noise.
- **Hit rate / success@k**: whether at least one relevant item is in the top k.
- **MRR** (mean reciprocal rank): average of 1/rank of the first relevant item; rewards putting the answer near the top.
- **nDCG@k**: rank-aware, handles graded relevance.

Example (illustrative): relevant chunks A, B; top-5 returns [X, A, Y, Z, W]. Recall@5 = 1/2, precision@5 = 1/5, MRR = 1/2.

Choose by need: recall@k for coverage, precision/nDCG for ordering, MRR for single-answer lookups. LLM-based context metrics (relevancy, recall) exist when chunk-level labels are unavailable.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Recall@k, precision@k, MRR, nDCG, plus RAG-flavoured contextual recall/precision. Know what each rewards. Interviews: compute a tiny example.

## How it works + one small example

Recall@k: fraction of relevant items in top k. Precision@k: fraction of the retrieved k that are relevant. MRR: 1/rank of first relevant. Contextual recall (RAGAS-style) asks if the retrieved set contains what the answer needs.

Do not report “accuracy” for ranking.

## Failure modes

1. **Precision-only so you reward tiny conservative k.**

2. **Recall-only so you reward dumping the corpus.**

3. **No labelled set, so you “metric” with a judge only.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I report Recall@k and a ranking-aware metric (MRR or nDCG) on a labelled set. Precision tells me about noise. I can compute a 3-item example on a whiteboard.

## A concrete walk-through

Gold {A,B}, retrieved [A,X,Y]. P@3=1/3, R@3=1/2 if both gold exist. You write that in the doc so the team shares a definition.

## Interview follow-up

They ask contextual vs classical. Contextual uses the question/answer; classical uses labelled chunks. Prefer labels when you have them.

## What I would measure

Whether the dashboard names @k and the label source.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Whether the dashboard names @k and the label source. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Recall@k, precision@k, MRR/nDCG. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: I report Recall@k and a ranking-aware metric (MRR or nDCG) on a labelled set. Precision tells me about noise. I can compute a 3-item example on a whiteboard. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask contextual vs classical. Contextual uses the question/answer; classical uses labelled chunks. Prefer labels when you have them. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Know what each rewards.
keyPoints: Labelled chunks beat judged “relevance” when possible.
Contextual metrics are not a substitute for labels.
Recall@k, precision@k, hit rate, MRR, nDCG
Recall guards against missing evidence; precision against noise

questions.q: Compute recall@5, precision@5 and MRR: relevant {A,B}, retrieved [X,A,Y,Z,W].
questions.a: Recall@5 = 1 of 2 = 0.5; precision@5 = 1 of 5 = 0.2; MRR = 1/rank of first relevant (A at rank 2) = 0.5.

questions.q: Which metric matters most for RAG coverage and why?
questions.a: Recall@k, because if relevant evidence is not retrieved the generator cannot answer groundedly; precision matters next to limit distracting noise.

questions.q: Relevant A,B; retrieved [A,X,Y]. Precision@3?
questions.a: 1/3 — one of three retrieved is relevant.

questions.q: Why not only precision?
questions.a: A system that returns one safe chunk scores 1.0 and misses the rest.

questions.q: What does MRR add?
questions.a: It cares how soon the first relevant chunk appears.

questions.q: No labels, only a judge of “relevance.” Caution?
questions.a: You are measuring a model’s opinion, not retrieval against gold. Use it as a proxy.

building-the-golden-dataset.explain:
## What it is

A RAG golden dataset contains **question, expected answer, and the supporting chunk or document IDs**.

Ways to build it:
- Sample real user questions and have a subject expert mark the correct passages and write the answer.
- Generate questions synthetically from chunks with an LLM (fast, scalable), then filter for quality and review a sample; synthetic questions tend to be too easy and lexically close to the chunk.
- Include multi-hop, ambiguous, unanswerable (should refuse) and out-of-scope questions.

Keep chunk IDs stable, or map answers to document-level IDs, otherwise re-chunking invalidates labels. Version the set, check labeller agreement, and keep a held-out part. Size: tens to hundreds with good coverage is more useful than thousands of similar items.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

RAG gold is queries, relevant chunks, and often ideal answers. You can hand-author, LLM-assist, or use a generator — then humans review. Synthetic questions that copy the chunk’s wording make retrieval too easy.

## How it works + one small example

Start 40 hand cases. Add LLM-proposed questions from chunks, then edit them to be less lexical. Store chunk ids, not just text, so index rebuilds do not orphan gold.

Unanswerable queries belong in the set.

## Failure modes

1. **Questions that quote the chunk.**

2. **No unanswerable items.**

3. **Gold answers written by the production model.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I curate query→chunk ids (and ideal answers) by hand and reviewed synthesis. I fight lexical overlap and I include unanswerable queries.

## A concrete walk-through

A synthetic set scored recall 0.96. You paraphrase the questions; recall drops to 0.61. That was the real retriever.

## Interview follow-up

They mention DeepEval synthetics. Fine as drafts; you still review.

## What I would measure

Lexical-overlap rate, unanswerable share, human-review rate.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Lexical-overlap rate, unanswerable share, human-review rate. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Gold: queries, chunk ids, optional ideal answers. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: I curate query→chunk ids (and ideal answers) by hand and reviewed synthesis. I fight lexical overlap and I include unanswerable queries. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They mention DeepEval synthetics. Fine as drafts; you still review. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Review synthetic items.

## What would change my mind

RAG gold is queries, relevant chunks, and often ideal answers. You can hand-author, LLM-assist, or use a generator — then humans review. Synthetic questions that copy the chunk’s wording make retrieval too easy. I change the design when a held-out slice moves, not when a demo is prettier. A third point that would force a redesign is: Paraphrase to avoid lexical giveaways. One counter-example that lives in the golden set beats a week of vibe testing.
keyPoints: Gold: queries, chunk ids, optional ideal answers.
Production model does not write gold answers.
Store question, reference answer and supporting chunk or doc IDs
Mix real and filtered synthetic questions, include unanswerable ones

questions.q: What does a RAG golden dataset contain?
questions.a: Questions, reference answers, and the IDs of supporting chunks or documents, plus types such as multi-hop, ambiguous and unanswerable questions, versioned and reviewed.

questions.q: Why can purely synthetic questions overstate retrieval quality?
questions.a: LLM-generated questions often copy wording from the source chunk, making them easy for lexical or embedding matching, unlike real user phrasing. Mix in real queries and review.

questions.q: Which synthetic-dataset weakness should you guard against?

questions.a: So a reindex does not orphan the gold text.

evaluating-the-generator-alone.explain:
## What it is

Test the generator by **fixing the context**: feed it known-good retrieved passages and judge the answer. This isolates generation quality from retrieval.

Checks: is the answer **faithful** to the context, does it **answer the question** (relevance and completeness), does it follow format and citation instructions, and does it correctly **refuse** when the context lacks the answer?

Useful variations: give the gold passage plus distractors (noise robustness), give conflicting passages, give no relevant passage (should abstain), and shuffle position of the relevant passage. If the generator fails with perfect context, change the prompt, model or output constraints; retrieval changes will not help.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Give the generator known-good context and see if it stays faithful and relevant. If it fails here, retrieval work will not save you. If it succeeds here and fails e2e, the context you actually assemble is the bug.

## How it works + one small example

Same questions, gold context, score faithfulness and answer relevance. Compare to the e2e context run. The delta is assembly/retrieval.

Do not sneak extra retrieved junk into this condition.

## Failure modes

1. **Calling e2e a generator eval.**

2. **Gold context that already contains the answer in the question.**

3. **No faithfulness metric, only vibe.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I eval the generator on gold context. Fail here → prompt/model. Pass here and fail e2e → retrieval or assembly.

## A concrete walk-through

Gold-context faithfulness 0.93, e2e 0.61. You stop rewriting the style prompt and fix the retriever.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about closed-book as a third condition. Useful as a hallucination baseline.

## What I would measure

Gold-context vs e2e delta.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Gold-context vs e2e delta. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Gold context isolates the generator. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: I eval the generator on gold context. Fail here → prompt/model. Pass here and fail e2e → retrieval or assembly. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about closed-book as a third condition. Useful as a hallucination baseline. detecting-unfaithful-answers.explain:
## What it is

An answer is **unfaithful** (hallucinated relative to context) if it contains claims not supported by the retrieved passages, even when they happen to be true in the world.

Detection approach (claim-level):
1. Break the answer into atomic **claims**.
2. For each claim, check with an LLM judge or an NLI model whether the context **entails** it.
3. Faithfulness score = supported claims / total claims.

Also inspect citations: does each cited passage really support the sentence? Flag unsupported numbers, names and dates especially. Pitfalls: the judge can accept plausible but unsupported claims, long contexts reduce judge accuracy, and paraphrases require semantic entailment. Calibrate with human labels on a sample. Mitigations: stricter prompts, citation requirements, answer-only-from-context rules and post-generation verification.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Unfaithful means claims not supported by the provided context: invented facts, ignored context, or mixed. Detect at claim level. A mostly-true paragraph can hide one lie.

## How it works + one small example

Split the answer into claims. For each: supported / unsupported / contradicting. Score = supported / total (or a weighted variant). Humans or a judge; calibrate the judge.

Citations that do not exist are a separate unfaithful class.

## Failure modes

1. **Sentence-level pass that hides a clause.**

2. **Treating “relevant” as “faithful.”**

3. **No check on citation existence.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I score faithfulness per claim against the provided context. A cited lie and an uncited truth fail different tests, but both are problems.

## A concrete walk-through

An answer of four claims, one invented. Sentence score looked fine. Claim score is 0.75 and you fail the case. The prompt is tightened.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about minor paraphrases. Supported includes faithful paraphrase, not copy-paste only.

## What I would measure

Claim-level unsupported rate, fabricated-citation rate.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Claim-level unsupported rate, fabricated-citation rate. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Faithfulness is per claim vs context. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: I score faithfulness per claim against the provided context. A cited lie and an uncited truth fail different tests, but both are problems. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about minor paraphrases. Supported includes faithful paraphrase, not copy-paste only. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Unsupported ≠ irrelevant.

One lie can hide in a good paragraph.
Unfaithful = claims not supported by the retrieved context

questions.q: How do you detect an unfaithful RAG answer?
questions.a: Extract atomic claims from the answer, verify each against the retrieved context with an entailment judge or NLI model, compute supported/total, and check that citations back each statement. Calibrate on human labels.

questions.q: An answer is factually true but not in the context. Is it faithful?
questions.a: No. Faithfulness is about support from the provided context; unsupported but true claims can't be verified from sources and may reflect memorisation or error.

questions.a: A single sentence can hide one unsupported claim; per-claim checks find it.

questions.a: No. Relevance is a different dimension.

questions.a: As an unfaithful/fabricated-citation fail even if the sentence sounds right.

questions.q: Must a faithful answer copy the chunk?
questions.a: No. Faithful paraphrase is allowed; invented facts are not.

component-tests-with-deepeval-ragas.explain:
## What it is

**DeepEval** and **RAGAS** are open-source libraries that provide ready-made RAG metrics and test harnesses. They implement metrics such as faithfulness, answer relevancy, context precision and recall, and (DeepEval) pytest-style test cases so evals run like unit tests in CI.

Typical use: build test cases of question, retrieved context, generated answer and optionally expected answer; select metrics with thresholds; run and inspect scores plus reasons. Both use an LLM as judge under the hood, so results depend on the judge model, cost tokens, and can be noisy.

Practical tips: pin the judge model and library version, calibrate against human labels, run component tests on retriever and generator separately, and check the current documentation because metric names and APIs evolve. Libraries save time but you still own dataset quality and thresholds.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

DeepEval and RAGAS give you metrics with names. You still have to know what each measures and what it does not. A library score is not a diagnosis. Interviews: pick one metric and define it in your words.

## How it works + one small example

Use them to implement component tests you already designed. Pin versions. Re-score a frozen batch when you upgrade the library. Read the doc for whether a metric is reference-based or a judge.

Write a one-pager: metric → definition → failure it catches.

## Failure modes

1. **Treating a 0.81 as truth without a definition.**

2. **Upgrading the library and celebrating a jump.**

3. **Using every metric they export.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I use DeepEval or RAGAS to run metrics I can define. I pin versions and I do not treat a library bump as a quality win.

## A concrete walk-through

A library upgrade jumps faithfulness 0.07. You re-score old traces; it is evaluator drift. You pin and write the delta down.

## Interview follow-up

They ask which to pick. Either; the definitions and pins matter more.

## What I would measure

Pinned versions, metrics you can define, upgrade-re-score done.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Pinned versions, metrics you can define, upgrade-re-score done. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Libraries implement metrics; you own definitions. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: I use DeepEval or RAGAS to run metrics I can define. I pin versions and I do not treat a library bump as a quality win. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask which to pick. Either; the definitions and pins matter more. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Pin versions.
keyPoints: Libraries implement metrics; you own definitions.
A jump after upgrade is suspect.
DeepEval and RAGAS give ready-made RAG metrics
DeepEval offers pytest-style tests for CI

questions.q: What do DeepEval and RAGAS provide?
questions.a: Prebuilt LLM-judged RAG metrics such as faithfulness, answer relevancy and context precision/recall, with test-case abstractions; DeepEval also integrates with pytest for CI thresholds.

questions.q: Your RAGAS scores shifted after a library upgrade. What do you do?
questions.a: Treat it as evaluator drift: pin library and judge model versions, re-score the same traces with old and new versions, and re-baseline before drawing conclusions about system quality.

questions.q: Scores jump after a metrics-library upgrade. First action?
questions.a: Pin versions and re-score identical traces to separate evaluator drift from system change.

questions.q: What must you know about each metric you enable?
questions.a: What it measures, whether it needs gold or a judge, and which failure it catches.

questions.q: Is a RAGAS number a diagnosis?
questions.a: No. It is a score. You still walk levels.

questions.q: Why not enable every exported metric?
questions.a: They overlap, cost money, and you will not know what moved.

the-full-retrieve-generate-pipeline.explain:
## What it is

Pipeline-level evaluation runs the whole **retrieve then generate** flow on real queries and scores the connection between steps. Component tests can pass while the pipeline fails because of interactions: the retrieved chunks are relevant yet too many, the generator ignores them, the prompt template truncates context, or query rewriting changes meaning.

Trace each run: query, rewritten query, retrieved chunks with scores, final prompt, answer. Score with reference-free metrics (the RAG Triad) and reference-based ones if gold answers exist. Compare pipeline variants (chunking, k, reranker, prompt) on the same dataset, and measure cost and latency of the whole pipeline.

This is where you find integration bugs: context window overflow, stale index, wrong metadata filters, or ordering effects.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Pipeline eval runs the real retrieve → assemble → generate path. It catches interaction bugs that isolated components miss: truncated context, lost-in-the-middle, order effects.

This is the “connected” test.

## How it works + one small example

Same cases as components, but the context is whatever the system actually built. Compare to gold-context generator scores. Inspect the assembled prompt on fails.

Log chunk ids that entered the prompt, not only what the retriever returned.

## Failure modes

1. **Assuming retriever top-k equals prompt contents.**

2. **No prompt dump on fail.**

3. **Skipping pipeline because components looked good.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I eval the real retrieve→assemble→generate path and I log what actually entered the prompt. Strong parts can still compose badly.

## A concrete walk-through

Retriever has the chunk; the assembler dropped it at 8k. Pipeline fails, components looked fine. You fix the budget.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about caching. Cache must be part of the pipeline condition if prod uses it.

## What I would measure

Pipeline vs component delta, dropped-chunk rate.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Pipeline vs component delta, dropped-chunk rate. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Pipeline uses the real assembled context. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: I eval the real retrieve→assemble→generate path and I log what actually entered the prompt. Strong parts can still compose badly. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about caching. Cache must be part of the pipeline condition if prod uses it. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Log ids that entered the prompt.

questions.q: Why is pipeline-level RAG evaluation needed after component tests?
questions.a: Components can each pass yet fail together due to truncation, ignored context, query rewriting changes or filter errors. Only end-to-end traced runs reveal those.

questions.q: What should you log for each pipeline run to debug later?
questions.a: Original and rewritten query, retrieved chunks with scores and IDs, the final assembled prompt, the model answer, token counts, latency and version identifiers.

questions.q: Retrieved chunk is correct but the answer ignores it. Fastest check?
questions.a: Inspect the assembled prompt for truncation or position, and test with gold context.

questions.q: Why can good components fail when connected?
questions.a: Assembly, order, truncation and distractors appear only in the pipeline.

questions.q: Retriever returned the chunk but the prompt does not have it. Whose bug?
questions.a: The assembler / budget, not the retriever.

questions.q: Should the pipeline condition use cache?
questions.a: Yes, if production does. Otherwise you measured a different path.

the-rag-triad.explain:
## What it is

The **RAG Triad** is three reference-free checks that together detect most RAG failures:

1. **Context relevance**: is the retrieved context relevant to the query?
2. **Groundedness (faithfulness)**: is the answer supported by the context?
3. **Answer relevance**: does the answer address the query?

Reading the triad: low context relevance means fix retrieval; low groundedness with good context means the generator is hallucinating; low answer relevance with grounded answers means the generator answered a different question or was vague. It works without gold answers so it fits production monitoring. Limitation: it does not check factual correctness against the world; a faithful answer from a wrong or outdated document passes.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

The triad is contextual relevancy (is the retrieved context on topic?), faithfulness (is the answer supported?), and answer relevance (does it address the question?). Together they diagnose more than any one score.

Interviews: define all three and a pattern (low relevancy + high faithfulness = faithful to junk).

## How it works + one small example

Compute all three on the same traces. Learn the patterns. Do not average them into one vanity number that hides the pattern.

A fourth operational column (latency, $) sits beside, not inside, the triad.

## Failure modes

1. **One blended “RAG score.”**

2. **Skipping relevancy because faithfulness looked fine.**

3. **Using the triad as safety.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

The triad is context relevancy, faithfulness, answer relevance. I read the pattern, I do not blend them into one vanity number.

## A concrete walk-through

Low relevancy, high faithfulness: you fix retrieval. High both, low answer relevance: you fix the question-following prompt.

## Interview follow-up

They ask origin. TruEra/RAG folklore — you care about the definitions, not the brand.

## What I would measure

Pattern-based actions taken, blended-score reports retired.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Pattern-based actions taken, blended-score reports retired. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Three: relevancy, faithfulness, answer relevance. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: The triad is context relevancy, faithfulness, answer relevance. I read the pattern, I do not blend them into one vanity number. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask origin. TruEra/RAG folklore — you care about the definitions, not the brand. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Read patterns, do not blend.
keyPoints: Low relevancy + high faith = faithful to junk.
High faith + low answer rel = grounded but off-topic.
Pattern of low scores points to retriever or generator

questions.q: What are the three parts of the RAG Triad and what do low values imply?
questions.a: Context relevance (low: retrieval problem), groundedness (low with relevant context: generator hallucination), answer relevance (low: the answer misses the question). Together they localise failures without gold answers.

questions.q: Triad scores are all high but users say answers are wrong. Why?
questions.a: The source documents may be wrong or outdated, so a faithful answer is still incorrect; or the judge is lenient. Add reference-based correctness checks and source freshness review.

questions.q: Triad shows low context relevance, high groundedness. Likely issue?
questions.a: Retrieval fetching irrelevant material while the answer sticks to it.

questions.q: Name the three triad legs.
questions.a: Contextual relevancy, faithfulness, answer relevance.

questions.q: Why not average them?
questions.a: Opposite diagnoses cancel in the mean.

questions.q: Is the triad a safety eval?
questions.a: No. Injection and PII are a different level.

contextual-relevancy.explain:
## What it is

**Contextual relevancy** measures how much of the retrieved context is relevant to the query. A judge examines each retrieved chunk (or statement) and marks whether it helps answer the question; the score is relevant over total.

Low contextual relevancy = **noise**: irrelevant chunks dilute the prompt, raise cost, and can mislead the generator. Closely related to context precision.

High relevancy doesn't mean the *needed* information is present; that is context **recall**/sufficiency, which needs a reference. So use both: relevancy for noise, recall for coverage.

Fixes for low relevancy: smaller k, reranking, score cutoffs, better chunking and metadata filters. Interview framing: relevancy is precision-like, recall is coverage-like.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Contextual relevancy asks whether the retrieved context is on topic for the question — precision-like, not “did we get every gold chunk.” High relevancy + low recall means clean but incomplete context.

## How it works + one small example

Judge or label: for each retrieved chunk, relevant or not. Aggregate. Use it next to recall. If you only have this, you can look precise while missing the deciding paragraph.

Do not confuse with answer relevance.

## Failure modes

1. **Using relevancy as a recall proxy.**

2. **Calling it faithfulness.**

3. **Scoring the answer instead of the chunks.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Contextual relevancy is whether the retrieved chunks are on topic. It is not recall and it is not answer relevance. I pair it with recall.

## A concrete walk-through

Relevancy 0.9, recall 0.4: you have clean junk-free misses. You raise candidate k and rerank, not the generator.

## Interview follow-up

They mix the words. You write the definitions on the dashboard.

## What I would measure

Relevancy next to recall on the same chart.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Relevancy next to recall on the same chart. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Relevancy ≈ precision of context. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: Contextual relevancy is whether the retrieved chunks are on topic. It is not recall and it is not answer relevance. I pair it with recall. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They mix the words. You write the definitions on the dashboard. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Pair with recall.

## What would change my mind

Contextual relevancy asks whether the retrieved context is on topic for the question — precision-like, not “did we get every gold chunk.” High relevancy + low recall means clean but incomplete context. I change the design when a held-out slice moves, not when a demo is prettier. A third point that would force a redesign is: Not faithfulness. One counter-example that lives in the golden set beats a week of vibe testing.
keyPoints: Share of retrieved context that is relevant to the query
Low score signals noise, cost and distraction

questions.q: What does contextual relevancy measure, and what does low mean?
questions.a: The proportion of retrieved context that is relevant to the query. Low means noisy retrieval that adds cost and distracts the generator; fix with reranking, smaller k or thresholds.

questions.q: Contextual relevancy is 0.95 but answers are incomplete. Which metric is missing?
questions.a: Context recall or sufficiency: relevant retrieved text may still lack some needed facts. Check coverage against the reference or required evidence.

questions.q: Contextual relevancy is high; recall is low. Meaning?
questions.a: Retrieved items are relevant but key evidence is missing.

questions.q: What is contextual relevancy?
questions.a: How on-topic the retrieved context is for the question.

questions.q: Can you use it instead of recall?
questions.a: No. You will miss incompleteness.

questions.q: Do you score the answer here?
questions.a: No. You score the chunks/context.

faithfulness.explain:
## What it is

**Faithfulness** (groundedness) measures whether every claim in the answer is supported by the retrieved context. Compute by decomposing the answer into claims and checking each against the context; score = supported claims / total claims.

What it catches: hallucinated details, outside-knowledge leakage, and over-generalisation. What it ignores: whether the answer is relevant, complete, or true in the real world.

A perfectly faithful answer can be useless ("The document does not mention that") or wrong if the source is wrong. Therefore pair it with answer relevance and correctness. For high-stakes domains require citations and verify them. Set thresholds per use case; legal or medical may need near 1.0 while casual chat can tolerate less.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Faithfulness: every claim in the answer is supported by the retrieved (or provided) context. It is not correctness versus the world. A faithful answer can be wrong if the context is wrong.

That distinction is the interview.

## How it works + one small example

Claim-split, support check against context only. Report unsupported rate. Do not give the judge the gold answer if you want this to stay faithfulness.

World-correctness is a different metric (factual correctness).

## Failure modes

1. **Calling faithfulness “accuracy.”**

2. **Letting the judge use world knowledge.**

3. **No claim split.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Faithfulness is support by the context, not truth in the world. I split claims and I do not let the judge use Wikipedia in its head.

## A concrete walk-through

Context has a stale rate. The answer repeats it. Faithfulness is 1.0, factual correctness is 0. You update the index, not the faithfulness prompt.

## Interview follow-up

They ask groundedness. Same idea; pick one word and stick to it.

## What I would measure

Unsupported-claim rate, judge-world-knowledge leaks in calibration.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Unsupported-claim rate, judge-world-knowledge leaks in calibration. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Faithful = supported by context. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: Faithfulness is support by the context, not truth in the world. I split claims and I do not let the judge use Wikipedia in its head. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask groundedness. Same idea; pick one word and stick to it. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Not world-correctness.

## What would change my mind

Faithfulness: every claim in the answer is supported by the retrieved (or provided) context. It is not correctness versus the world. A faithful answer can be wrong if the context is wrong. That distinction is the interview. I change the design when a held-out slice moves, not when a demo is prettier. A third point that would force a redesign is: Claim-level. One counter-example that lives in the golden set beats a week of vibe testing.

questions.q: Define faithfulness and how it is computed.
questions.a: Fraction of the answer's atomic claims entailed by the retrieved context, found by claim decomposition and a judge or NLI check against the context.

questions.q: Can an answer score 1.0 faithfulness and still be bad?
questions.a: Yes: it can be irrelevant, trivially cautious, incomplete, or faithful to a wrong or outdated source. Combine with relevance, completeness and correctness metrics.

questions.q: Faithfulness 1.0 and the fact is wrong. How?
questions.a: The context was wrong or stale. Faithfulness does not check the world.

questions.a: Outside knowledge or the gold answer, if you want faithfulness not correctness.

questions.q: Faithfulness vs factual correctness?
questions.a: Context support vs world/gold truth.
